A journal article published in April of 2020 showcased the results of a survey sent out online from which 10,754 individuals in Iran, from all 31 provinces, have participated in. The survey focuses on anxiety levels of the general population of Iran since the start of the pandemic. Specific parts of the population experience higher anxiety than others. This includes higher anxiety among women (95 % CI [0.1, 81.36], p < 0.001), people who follow COVID-19 related news  (p < 0.001), people who fall under the age group of  21–40 years (p < 0.001), people who live in high COVID-19 prevalence provinces, and finally, individuals who have family members or friends that are COVID-19 positive (95 % CI [1.2, 35.03], p < 0.001). It states that the last group might fear contracting the virus which explains the anxiety they feel. It is clear that the pandemic has an impact on anxiety levels among the general population of Iran, however it is unclear whether the individuals who were surveyed experienced an 'increase' specifically. One can deduct that it did 'increase' their anxiety levels but it does not specifically state so and rather focuses on the specific groups within the population that experiences anxiety during the pandemic. Furthermore, the impact is government driven as the US sanctions posed on Iran has influenced the government's ability to provide the necessary healthcare services. Behavioural changes also have an impact as the survey showed that people who follow the COVID-19 related news experience higher anxiety levels. Take note that this indicator is localized since most of the participants (66.7%) of the survey comes from high prevalent COVID-19 provinces  (Tehran, Qom, Isfahan, and Mazandaran). The remaining participants come from the other provinces and therefore includes a degree of the entire nation but is mostly localized.

A questionnaire was sent out by researchers with a response from 500 Israelis in late April relating to mental health of the population sample. It was found that almost a quarter of the sample expressed that they have a high or very high level of anxiety due to COVID-19, based on a rating of their anxiety level on a scale of 1 to 5. 12% of the sample were at risk for major depression. The results showed that people were worried about their health or their family's health, or they felt economic stress because of lockdown regulations. The researchers stated that "...we found that those people with higher levels of worry and stress because of COVID-19 also had much higher levels of anxiety and depression." The researchers therefore concluded that "the higher levels of anxiety and depression risk were the result of the coronavirus." It is therefore likely that mental health concerns and consequences are increasing among the Israeli population due to concerns caused by COVID-19.

Poor households in both urban and rural areas of the DRC have lost key sources of income. The lose of income in poor households is driven by the restriction put in place to contain the spread of the virus. These restrictions include the closure of international and provincial borders, curfews and the closure of businesses and schools. Although some of these restrictions were eased from the 15th of August by easing of movement and restrictions and reopening schools and businesses, poor households access to income and food remain affected by those previously enacted restrictions. The demand from income generating activities in the DRC remain low which continues to put strain on households which were dependent on that source of income. In addition there is a decline in the demand for informal labour and reduced ability to engage in informal trade putting those dependent (typically the poor) on these activities for income at a disposed source of income.
source: FEWS NET Famine Early Warning Systems Network

justification:
Informal cross border trade activities have declined along border points. Poor farmers within DRC have been negatively affected by the COVID-19 restrictions implemented by the government. Negative impacts have risen from border closures which has limited trade flows in agricultural inputs which normally would be imported from neighboring countries. This is expected to result in decreased area planted, less/fewer agricultural labor opportunities and below average season B production. Due to slowed down domestic trade in both rural and urban areas, farmers (rural farmers) may find it difficult to sell their goods therefore resulting in lower income from sales. Movement restrictions and reduced global demand has led foreign currency shortages due to the reduction in exports of tobacco, coffee, cacao and industrial metals. This has resulted in the increase in prices of good. Maize prices in Kinshasa in July were  reported nearly 80% higher than it was in February. 
Supply chains and market functioning are being disrupted with the reduction in the availability of food and non-food products. The rising market prices and decline in the availability and access to food is contributing to the deterioration in food and nutrition security.
indicator: Ability of international food supply chain to support domestic food availability
source: FEWS NET Famine Early Warning Systems Network

The New Humanitarian reported that a great number of Mexicans have been forced from their homes by the brutality of gang violence of the country, during the coronavirus pandemic. Fighting between myriad armed groups has intensified since March, with criminals taking advantage of a COVID-19 lockdown to force hundreds more people from their villages. 
The day after the lockdown, “violence displaced around 800 people, increasing the risk to the community from COVID-19, in addition to the impacts in terms of access to food, adequate housing, drinking water, and health services,” Brenda Pérez, advocate on internal displacement for Mexico’s Commission for the Defense and Promotion of Human Rights, said in a message to the UN Human Rights Council in July. 
Also, due to the lack in governmental support and high levels of authorities corruption, many Mexicans have decided to follow migrants and asylum seekers on their route north to the US border, with increasingly uncertain outcomes.
The drivers of this change are both "Behavioral changes" and "Governmental Measures" due to multiple factors that participate in the increase of Internal displacement in Mexico, which summarizing are the lack of social and financial support from the Government to the most vulnerable categories of the population, as well as the strong impact that non-state armed groups have on this indicator.

Certainly, the mobility restrictions due to COVID-19 have had a direct effect on the migration projects of people, both due to the closure of borders, as well as the quarantine, isolation and social distancing measures that have been established in the different countries of the region. However, these restrictions appear to have only delayed possible migrations.
Also, during the pandemic, the United States and Mexico tightened measures to curb the entry of migrants. The government of Donald Trump, for example, suspended until the end of May the permanent residence visas that they gave to legal migrants, has expelled about 10,000 immigrants.

The suspension of non-essential activities of the public, private and social sectors was ordered to mitigate the spread and transmission of Covid-19. The services exempt from suspension were medical and health services, public security and sectors essential for the economy. The measures were to last until April 30, however, on April 20 they were extended until May 30. On June 1, the Mexican government began easing nationwide restrictions and started phasing in non-essential economic activities in some states and municipalities using a national “stoplight” system, according to the trend of new cases in different areas. Six states are designated “red”, which means that only essential activities are allowed. Essential activities include:  the provision of medical services and supplies, grocery delivery services, operation of grocery stores, restaurant delivery and carryout services, assurance of public safety, maintenance of fundamental economic functions and government social programs, work in critical infrastructure, construction, and manufacturing of transportation equipment. Hotels are limited to 25 percent occupancy for guests working on critical activities.  Parks are also limited to 25 percent occupancy. Twenty-five states are designated “orange”. Under orange, hotels, restaurants, barber shops, open-air parks, and gyms are limited to 50 percent capacity.  Markets and supermarkets will operate at 75 percent capacity. Additionally, shopping malls, churches, cinemas, theaters, museums, and cultural events will be limited to 25 percent capacity.
One state is designated “yellow”. Under yellow, all work activities are permitted.  Public space may open on a regular basis, while enclosed public spaces can open with reduced capacity. 
Schools are closed and all electoral processes, censuses, and surveys are postponed until further notice.
source: U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Mexico

In poor ccountries such as the DRC covid-19 impacts are felt drastically on the poor. With the current limitation of information and data about COVID-19s impact on child marriage, countries like the DRC can draw valuable information from experiences of other pandemics such as Ebola. These experiences suggest that girls and women are the ones adversely affected by such a crisis especially those who find themselves within poor households and marginalized groups. Child marriage is often driven by circumstances where family and community structures are broken down during a crisis and displacement. Child marriage will therefore be driven by the challenges the pandemic will create such as the loss of household income, higher risk of violence in the household and lack of access to schooling. Therefore child marriage will be seen as patching these challenges in order to overcome them. In other instances, marriage is supposedly seen as protection from for girls and their families from the social stigma that can result from surviving rape or sexual assault. The specific drivers of child marriage are therefore poverty, pandemics, adolescent pregnancy and armed conflict.

The executive director of the Family Health Association Iran (FHA Iran) held an interview providing some insight into the sexual and reproductive services available in Iran during the pandemic. Usually there are sexual and reproductive healthcare (SRH) services such as contraception, safe abortion, HIV/AIDS and STI treatment, gynecology and obstetrics services available in Iran- for vulnerable groups. These services are provided through static and integrated clinics- and usually there are "six static and integrated clinics, and one mobile clinic. Since the outbreak we have been able to provide SRHR services via three static clinics, and one outreach team." Therefore the amount of clinics available have decreased in Iran. What is even more notable is that the Family Health Association (FHA) are restricted in providing these services: "We are only allowed to provide contraceptives for vulnerable groups such as refugees, sex workers, substance users, and people living with HIV." Contraceptives are not allowed to be given to Iranian people (who are not vulnerable) due to government regulations that aims to combat Iran's decreasing population. It would seem that Iranian people are in anyway restricted in using sexual and reproductive services- irrespective of the pandemic. According to the article midwifery services that require a physical presence have also been hard hit in Iran. Furthermore, the U.S. sanctions have also limited funding which affected staff salaries and equipment for providing these services. I also labelled the affect that COVID-19 has on the indicator as 'behavioral' since: "It would seem during crisis settings, SRHR becomes less of a priority for people. They are more concerned with remaining safe and free from the virus." People are therefore less likely to reach out to the services provided due to the virus. justification: The governmental regime in Iran favors those who are Shi’a Muslims and Persian speakers. They receive privileges from the regime (not stated what privileges) and are perceived to be located in Tehran and other areas that are perceived as the "Persian center". The minorities in Iran are 10% of the Iranian population that is Sunni Muslim rather than Shi’a who are largely non-Persian. Other ethnic minorities are Kurds, Baluchis, and Arabs, in addition to non-Shi’a and non-Muslim religious minorities. These minorities have faced greater discrimination during COVID-19 and an example thereof was during the releasing of prisoners in March of 2020. To quote: "...during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, prisoners in Tehran were prioritized, and therefore ethnic minorities were far less likely to see freedom." The Persians in Iran were prioritized over the minorities in other prisons for release (release for fear of spreading of COVID-19). Although the release of prisoners is overall controversial, those who were prioritized received greater benefits than the minority prisoners who are now at greater risk of being exposed to COVID-19. Furthermore the report also talks about the Afghan refugees, that also make up for minorities in Iran. They are restricted in their movement, even before the pandemic, as 27/31 of the provinces ban residence of Afghans. It is unsure whether discrimination has increased towards the refugees since the pandemic.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification: Minorities in Iran (non-Persians) reside in the border provinces of Iran. Persians are concentrated in Iran’s central cities, including the capital Tehran. By knowing this, it was possible to see from both the published and unofficial reports that there is a higher COVID-19 fatality rate in Iran’s non-Persian provinces than the Persian concentrated center. This trend is consistent with the fact that there are less hospital beds available in the non-persian provinces (that is lower below the national average). In Persian populated provinces there are more beds available than the national average. The Iranian health system averages 155 hospital beds for every 100,000 people. Some of the non-Persian provinces who have averages below that average includes  the Azerbaijani populated provinces (140 beds), in the Baluch (99 beds) and Kurd (143 beds) populated provinces. In contrast, Persian populated provinces have over 200 beds (which is above the average). It is therefore clear that ethnic minority groups (i.e. non-Persians) have less access to medical equipment such as hospital beds, which directly correlates with the higher mortality rate among the Iranian minorities.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

1. direct employees reduce their days/hours of work or not to attend work at all;

According to the Interior Ministry, reported cases of domestic violence increased since the beginning of the COVID-19 quarantine (March-June 2020). 7,669 cases were reported in April, in May the figure rose to 11,808 and in June it reached 14,404. 
Also, according to BBC, from March 16 to June 30, 915 people were reported missing, of which 70% were of girls and adolescents. Considering that during the lockdown, no mechanisms to make complaints of missing persons, the real number is probably higher than the official one.

In Peru records show a decrease in child labour between 2012 and 2018, going from an employment rate of children and adolescents of 31.7% to 26.1%, which is equivalent to a reduction of 5.6 percentage points (ENAHO, 2018). There is no data available regarding child labour since the beginning of the pandemic in Peru, for this reason, it was logged as info gap. Estimations indicate that the rate of child labour could increase oscillating between 1 and 3 percentage points, as due to the GDP contraction, the consequent increase in unemployment and poverty will severely affect the wellbeing of families. The most vulnerable categories, of which young people and children, who represent a significant proportion of persons in unprotected and informal employment, will be those most affected by the deterioration of the economy. Also, low coverage of social protection, lack of access to social security and higher levels of poverty are possible drivers of the increase in child labour.
source: International Labour Organization - Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean

justification: An increase in child marriages has been predicted in Latin America and the Caribbean, mainly as a consequence of school closures and economic collapse due to the COVID-19 emergency; precise data relating to Peru are not yet available, thus it has been indicated as an info gap.

According to a media source, seven out of ten people in Peru are faced with a significant increase in anxiety or stress, due to the fear of infection from the novel-coronavirus. Other causes responsible of the increased mental health problems related with the lockdown, are the increased state of unemployment, the limited financial protection and support for those employed in the informal sector (70% of the population), or the fact that many students were forced to abandon their studies, or the increased work and responsibilities at home for many families.
The situation is aggravated for Venezuelan migrants in Peru that, mostly due to the economic difficulties faced because of the COVID-19 lockdown, faced increased rates of anxiety and depression in April 2020 rather than those registered upon arrival in Peru in August 2019. Half of women presenting anxiety disorder symptoms and nearly two in five men. Overall, one in three met the clinical definition for depression. In other words, one month of the quarantine did more to affect the mental health of a population than their desperation-driven migration the previous year from Venezuela.

According to National Center for Biotechnology Information (a governmental source), the cases of human rights violations by authorities have increased during the COVID-19 state of emergency (March-April 2020). The explanation of the increase of this indicator is that the Government of Peru has legislated policies to enforce physical distancing by restricting the mobility of its citizens based on binary understandings of gender, meaning that on alternating days women are allowed to access essential services and on the other days, men. People and communities that exist outside of hegemonic understandings of binary gender presentation and identities were excluded from the policy. The implementation and policing of these binary, gender-based laws have resulted in direct violence perpetrated against transgender communities.
This event represents an abuse of human rights by the authorities and is therefore directly caused by Governmental measures.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: According to the World Bank, there is evidence of an increase in violence and discriminatory treatment directed at sexual and gender minorities, and to member of the LGBT+ community during the COVID-19 emergency (March-June 2020). Although the source reported the increase of this indicator as a COVID-19 impact, the reason of the change is unclear, and therefore the driver is logged as "undetermined".
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification:
According to the National Center for Biotechnology Information, reported cases of stigma from the authorities have increased since the COVID-19 state of emergency in Peru (March-April 2020), due to the implementation of gender-based policy to reinforce social distancing, which has affected negatively the Peruvian transgender community. 
Events of public humiliation of  LGBT+ community members by the police have been reported, including physical assault, gender policing, and other transphobic actions.
Also, according to a media source, indigenous communities in Peru are faced with discrimination by authorities. According to a letter from natives to the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, the Government is not providing adequate support and protection to these communities during the pandemic.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

According to a media, the availability of (non-COVID-19 related) medical supply in Peru has decreased since mid-March 2020, as a direct consequence of the novel-coronavirus pandemic.  
The driver of this change is logged as "Governmental Measures" as the change is due to the under-investment on public health. The country spent 3.165% of GDP on public health in 2017, according to the World Bank. Peru also has less than two hospital beds per 1,000 people, which is insufficient to face a health crisis. Lack of basic hygiene products, health professionals and hospital equipment and beds has affected mostly the most vulnerable communities such as the indigenous from the Amazons.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: Despite the global covid 19 pandemic peoples access to local markets, entrepreneurs and local products has grown. The Togolese government has also encouraged the population to consume local products by buying rice and cereals from farmers and making them available to the population at lower prices compared to rice from Thailand, Vietnam or China. Therefore local entrepreneurs also able to continue selling their product.
There is no information related to how the domestic food supply chain (labour force) has been impacted by the covid 19 pandemic in Togo

As a result, many pregnant women have reported feeling very anxious. Lady health workers also lacked correct PPE and couldn’t travel as freely as they were able to so they couldn’t carry out their usual routine house visits and so many women lack access to contraception. Government hospitals across the country including Karachi suspended all post-partum family planning counselling session.

In addition to this, many sources point to the inability of domestic food supply due to the unaffordable or unavailable petrol for the population (e.g.: many peasants cannot afford to take their production to collection and distribution points, making more urbanised areas susceptible to food shortages), this trend is likely reflected on international chains. justification: Fuel shortages around Venezuela have caused many difficulties to harvest food and deliver from production to consumption points, breaking supply chains and consequently impacting the econonmy and health of the population. In addition to these, restrictions to open markets have been imposed (e.g. temporary closure of Las Pulgas and Coche markets); (->US blocking petrol to Venezuela). Nevertheless, GICOS (2020) inform 70% of people report food availability (physically in markets) but unaffordable.

Not much information was found on the state of markets at a national level. Nevertheless, important markets, that constitute crucial points to sell and buy food, were restricted in big cities with high levels of Covid-19 positive cases. Las Pulgas market in Maracaibo, considered an "epicentre" for Covid-19 contagion, was closed for 3 months, impacting the livelihoods and access to food for an important part of the population. Likewise, Coche market in Caracas, also essential to feed and provide income of an important number of people, is restricted to open 3 days (instead of 6) since the beginning of containment measures in March.

School feeding programmes were affected by the closure of schools in March for the prevention of COVID-19. According to some sources, the state's "School Feeding Programme" (Programa de Alimentación Escolar) are still active and offering food to kids and adyacent communities (Xinhuan News). According to the opposition and other informants, the statal programme did not get to cover the majority of schools even prior to the pandemic (France24).

Other private initiatives, like those from UNICEF (La Educación No Puede Esperar - Education cannot wait), religious volunteers and former feeding centers are now covering these needs prioritising kids and their families, preparing food and delivering basic ingredients as well as school kits.

Even if there are no exact figures on employment for Venezuela, according to UN News (https://news.un.org/es/story/2020/06/1476782) Latin America is the region where more jobs have been lost due to the pandemic. It is reported that industries have been stopped or reduced due to containment measures but also due to the country's economic collapse (inflation, petrol shortages, US blockade, etc.), so formal employment is expected to have declined. Moreover, people also report re-opening businesses informally during quarantine to access to some sort of income, affecting the number of formal employment.
The government has implemented a plan to support workers (Sistema Patria, bono "Quédate en casa"), but this aid is reported insufficient to cover all applicants.

There are no official figures on the informal sector since 2018. The "informal sector union" (Sintrandecos) states almost 70% of workers in Venezuela are in the informal sector, likely to increase out of necessity and containment measures of the pandemic (formal workers now forced to work informally, more people need to access some sort of income due to reduction in remittances, overall collapse, etc.). Nevertheless, informal workers are also now more chased by authorities as lockdown measures are enforced (for instance, in food markets that are only partially open). The government has implemented a plan to support workers, also those in the informal sector (Sistema Patria, bono "Quédate en casa"), but this aid is reported to fall short to cover all applicants.

Remittances are a key source of income for many families in Venezuela. The diaspora has been very harshly striken by COVID-19 containment measures globally and overall economic recessions, many being unable to send any money home and even returning to Venezuela facing hard conditions, especially in neighbouring countries like Colombia and Brazil.

Hyperinflation has remained a trend since November 2017 (Lexology), and the bolivar has even "lost its exchange function" due to the depreciation, leading to a "dollarisation" of the economy (the US dollar as the common currency). These trends have deepened with Trump's economic and financial sanctions and general COVID-19 crisis (Aljazeera).
The constant inflation and lack of access to US dollars that were already an obstacle to most Venezuelan populations have now aggravated with COVID-19 containment measures (lockdown and most productive activities at lower rate), increased prices of imported goods and gasoline shortages.

According to a local media source, the provision of public services did not report change since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-May 2020), as the Government adopted measures aimed at guaranteeing the access and continuity of public services during the emergency. As reported by the source, the main measures taken by the authorities were to provide the continuity of telecommunications and electricity services.

As of March 2020, Qatar's Primary Health Care Corporation (PHCC) suspended all non-essential services, which amounted to the cancelling of 77,927 scheduled
appointments. However, to accommodate patients who have lost their 'non-essential' in-person appointments, Qatar offered 'telemedicine' consultations to patients who previously had appointments. The article stated that home medication refill delivery services for elderly, noncommunicable disease patients, and pregnant
women were also introduced at the end of March 2020.  Therefore, although in-person appointments/services were largely cancelled in Qatar, the country catered for the population's needs through telecommunication and delivery services of medicine. When it came to patients with emergencies and essential health needs; urgent services, walk in clinics, laboratories and pharmacy diagnostics were all open and operating. I therefore labelled this indicator as having 'no change' in the availability of services, although COVID-19 did drive the change in restructuring the healthcare system initially.

We are already seeing a shortage of fresh fruit and vegetables from the Highlands in the cities, but not yet a shortage of imported food. Other non-food items are still arriving in PNG with only a slight delay,” Rice told OBG.
One factor working in PNG’s favour is that local food manufacturers have long maintained large raw-material inventories, to hedge against shipping disruptions or foreign exchange shortages.

While Covid-19 containment measures will have a detrimental effect on overall economic activity, there are signs that well-known local food brands may experience an upturn in PNG, at least in the short-term: Paradise Foods reported that sales during the last two weeks of March were 20% higher than expected, as urban residents stocked up on provisions.

Restrictions imposed on travel and closure of businesses during the SoE limited, and in some cases prevented, access to essential goods and services with major impacts on food supply chains. While some shops and markets were permitted to remain open, police have not adequately facilitated implementation, impacting the livelihoods of both rural and urban households. Rural produce has not reached urban markets, similarly urban supplies have not reached rural and outlying provinces. Limited supply drives prices up, making crucial supplies too expensive for ordinary citizens.

Restrictions have also led to job losses and a drastic fall in incomes. This has disproportionately affected a higher proportion of households that are already disadvantaged, both economically and socially. The poor cannot stock up on food and have no savings for emergencies so without work there is no money. This translates to thousands of informal enterprises and livelihoods lost.

Less disposable income makes it harder to afford basic needs for survival. Most people struggle to meet daily needs in ordinary times, so it is extremely hard for households to cope for weeks and or even months without a regular income. Many are going without food and this is a catalyst for creating additional social issues: domestic violence over household finances; increased theft; and petty crime driven by hunger and starvation. Poor diet and nutrition weaken the body’s natural defense system and leave the poor and disadvantaged susceptible to disease.
source: Asia and the Pacific Policy Society

No reports pertain to particular violence that migrants have undergone but they are subject to increased vulnerability.  When viewing the alternative source, a Nepali man who was arrested stated that “The jail was full of people…. All the people were fed in a group, with food lying on plastic on the floor. Some were not able to snatch the food because of the crowd.” This treatment may emphasise that migrant workers face discrimination, however it is not 100% certain if it had increased amidst COVID-19. Migrant workers make up 60% of the population in Qatar but can be interpreted as the 'minority' as they are subject to marginalization and discrimination. Before and during the pandemic these migrant workers are subject to being paid below the minimum wage, making them unable to afford health insurance in Qatar, transportation to healthcare centers, and the inability of affording healthcare cards. Therefore, their access to healthcare is severely limited because of the discrimination they face. Unfortunately because of this discrimination of living in appalling conditions, the migrant workers are most vulnerable to COVID-19 as they live in crowded, unhygienic conditions. Amidst the pandemic, coalition of non-governmental organizations requested that migrant workers have better access to healthcare in Qatar. The Qatari government therefore issued a few changes so that migrants receive proper treatment during the COVID-19 pandemic. One of the steps they have taken is transforming the Hazm Mebaireek General Hospital, which lies in the Industrial Area of Qatar (where migrants live), into a COVID-19 health facility. This indicator was therefore labelled as 'undetermined' as it is unsure whether migrant workers have now received increased access to healthcare since before the pandemic they were unable to afford to do so. It is unsure if all the migrants now have access to this COVID-19 facility or only those who live in that area. Furthermore, because of their inability to pay for healthcare (before the pandemic) it is unsure to what extent do migrants have to pay for expenses in relation to COVID-19. Although access to healthcare seem to have increased in their area it is unsure to what extent = undetermined.

Brasil is the main country from which the repatriation took place, followed by Argentina, Uruguay, Bolivia, Chile, Mexico and Panama. 
The main drivers of this repatriation of Paraguayans during the pandemic, is the complicated economic scenario and the fragile health system found in the host countries such as Brasil and Argentina. Excessive force was used against migrant workers in Qatar which took away their freedom. According to the source "The police told most of the men that they were going to be tested for COVID-19 and would be returned to their accommodation afterwards. Instead, they were taken to detention centres and held in appalling conditions for several days, before being sent to Nepal." The men received no explanation for why they were treated this way and why they were put on planes to exit the country. One can infer that it is due to the fear of the spread of COVID-19 where the migrant population was targeted by authorities. Furthermore when viewing the alternative source, the Industrial area (where many migrants live) has gone under total lockdown where the migrant workers cannot leave or enter the area. It is described as being a 'virtual prison', where fear and panic is apparent among the workers. To a certain extent, it is understandable why the lockdown has occurred, since the virus is spreading in this area. Yet it would seem that the workers are forced to live under appalling conditions within the lockdown and since it is only enforced where they live, it seems to have stripped them off their rights, where they are subject to discrimination. It is should be noted that the lockdown in the industrial area has been lifted, but it is apparent that excessive force was used due to the impacts of COVID-19.

justification:
The Papua New Guinea (PNG) Nurses Association organized a sit-in protest on March 26, 2020 to protest the lack of measures and equaipment to protect them against COVID-19.

The PNG government imposed a two-week lockdown on March 23 to contain the spread of the novel coronavirus, the virus that causes the potentially fatal COVID-19 disease. At the time of writing, PNG has only one positive COVID-19, case but authorities have identified 3,000 “persons of interest”, of which 2,230 are being actively monitored. PNG has a population of almost nine million.

The PNG Nurses Association raised the concern on March 6 that most hospitals do not have isolation units for handling COVID-19 patients and bemoaned the inadequate public health measures aimed at controlling the spread of the disease.

After the announcement of the lockdown, the PNG Nurses Association reiterated its concern about the absence of proper training and mechanisms at community level to deal with the disease.

The group petitioned the government to provide nurses with personal protective equipment (PPE), risk and travel allowances, food rations, and insurance.

After the breakdown of negotiations, the group called a strike at Port Moresby General Hospital, National Capital District Health Authority, and Laloki Public Psychiatric Hospital outside the capital city of Port Moresby.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

Although a news article did state that there are reports of an increase in forced child marriage due to school closures and economic strains (caused by COVID-19). The indicator was still marked as an infogap, since it is not certain that child marriages have indeed increased. Child/forced marriage is defended as being part of the culture and rises during Ramadan to have help with cooking and chores in families.

Since the begin of the COVID-19 Pandemic there was a 35% increase in reports of domestic violence in Cameroon. This is mostly violence against women which is caused by stress and increased alcohol consumption of their partner due the pandemic. The stress is caused by job loss or scared of getting sick.

According to OCHA the access of reproductive services for women has decrease due to the lack of resources such as health professional, contraceptives, and SRHR services while fighting COVID-19. It has also become expensive to provide or buy contraceptives so it indicates an increase in pregnancy.

justification: There is no relevant information regarding a change of reported discriminations of specific groups. The Government is attempting to create peace but the community does not want to covert the area to French-speaking only. These groups are the minority in the country.

justification: There are no relevant reports regarding the change in number or patterns of human trafficking for 2020 in Cameroon.

This indicator was considered an infogap because there is no relevant data on the changes in child labour since the pandemic started. There is no source date available.

There are restrictions placed on the UN to support regions in the North, due to the Civil war. There was also no way to inform these high risk areas of COVID-19 due to the risk of entry. There is no specific information regarding groups that don't have access to COVID-19 support which is why this indicator is considered an infogap.

justification: Overcrowded prisons are seen in many regions in Cameroon. As of 15 April 2020 Cameroon prisons have released hundreds of detainees (831 in one prison and 214 in the Maroua prison) in the the Far North Region, due to overcrowded prisons. They were released in fear of risking COVID-19 infection and spread thereof. In the far Northern region, the number of prisoners have decreased from 3 370 to 2 547 detainees. It is clear that the incarceration rate is decreasing due to the direct result of fear of COVID-19 infection and spread in prisons.

There is no relevant information on change in violence of health workers in Cameroon since the beginning of the pandemic. Given this, the indicator has an infogap. However, it should be noted that since 2016, in the North-West and South-West regions, health related facilities, such as hospitals were affected by violent groups. Anglophone regions only function with 34% of health facilities
There is no relevant information on the changes of civil unrest that relate to COVID-19 in Cameroon. Therefore this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: According to BBC News and Human Rights Watch there is unrest that started protests in the Far North of Cameroon since 2017. These protests and war are due to a certain region being English-orientated, where the government is pressuring these regions to incorporate more French-oriented schools, wanting the region to become more French-speaking. These protests do not seem to have decreased since the COVID-19 pandemic. There are no relevant information on the exact changes of these activities, indicating an infogap.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification: Overall, there is a lack of information pertaining to changes of human rights abuse in Cameroon, indicating an infogap. However, it should be noted that there are poor services and conditions in detention centers in Cameroon. Inmates have the right to be informed of COVID-19 and need access to the appropriate healthcare, yet it is stated that there is a lack of information given to prisoners regarding COVID-19. Moreover, political activists are being detained for criticising the government of Cameroon, and the president, which indicates the abuse of authorities.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: The national election was held in February of 2020 before the first case was reported in Cameroon. This election was previously postpone due to unrest during December 2019. There are no records of other elections held during the pandemic, making this indicator not applicable.
indicator: Elections taking place as scheduled pre-COVID

justification: According to UNAIDS, an interview with Savania which has been Cameroon's country director for the UNAIDS, stated that she has seen a rise in discriminations and stigma with population groups in Cameroon but it was not specified which group. Given the lack of information, this indicator was considered an infogap.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification: The Cameroonian 2020 National election took place on the 9th of February before restrictions were placed in the country. Although there was a decrease in voters turnout where the 2020 election had a decrease of more that 30% than the 2013 election, there is no indication this is caused by the pandemic. Given that the election (and voter turnout) occurred before the pandemic, this indicator is not applicable. No source date is provided.
indicator: Voter turnout in latest national elections that took place since beginning of covid pandemic

justification: There is no relevant information on the change of access to people in need relating to COVID-19 in Cameroon. However, a news article did indicated that there were restrictions in an UN flight to assist people in need in Cameroon, specifically in the north of the country. Not enough information is given on the specific change in access, therefore this indicator has an infogap.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: There is no specific detailed information regarding the change in the population's  access to humanitarian service in Cameroon. Therefore, this indicator has an infogap. Although a news article reported that a humanitarian flight has been ground due to violence unrelated to COVID-19. Only after the 8th of April did the government allow the UN workers and Medical aid to help people in need in Cameroon.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification: There is no relevant information on the privations of public services in Cameroon since the pandemic starte.

There is no relevant report on the change of IO/INGO in Cameroon. There is no indication that these organisation have decrease or increase their funding or support for Cameroon during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Human Rights Office received a video showing the actions of Grupo Lince's agents in a control carried out on public roads, which would constitute an abuse of authority during the quarantine controls in the face of the advance of the coronavirus. Consequently, the prosecutor Silvia Cabrera intervened and requested reports on the actions carried out by the motorized police officers.
Dozens of videos recording these these abuses of power became viral on the internet, showing agents from the "Grupo Lince" forcing people who fail to comply with quarantine measures to perform exercises, or ridicule themselves in public, even reporting cases of extreme violence on public roads. 
The Minister of the Interior, Euclides Acevedo, described as acts of "creativity" by the police, considerably diminishing the extent of these events.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: No significant data reported on stigmatization on specific groups by the authorities since the beginning of the pandemic.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification:
The Ministry of Education and Sciences (MEC) is carrying out the distribution of food kits to students, in order to replace the school feeding programs for the schools and colleges  in the capital. This Programme is named "Mi almuerzo escolar en familia", and it has been developed as a result of the measures adopted to face the health emergency due to the risk of expansion of COVID-19 at the national level, therefore the delivery work is implemented under strict prevention measures and protocols. 400 people participated in the distribution operations, of which 150 were Police Officers, 160 Military Officers plus a large number of MEC officials.
This school feeding program was delivered in accordance with the return to academic activities after winter break. 
At the end of the first week of home-schooling and after four days of distribution, the MEC reached 97 schools, delivering 22,102 kits, representing 344,768 kg. These data and informations only refer to the city of Asunción, and no data is available for other Paraguayan cities or rural areas. Therefore, the indicator has been logged as a localized impact.

No reports available regarding the availability of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies in Paraguay during the pandemic.
A local media reported lack of basic medications, such as gauzes and gloves, and other medical supplies, due to problems with the management of medical material available in hospitals, which was not correctly quantified by the software used for counting the stock of medical equipment. 
Despite this situation, no emergency cases of lack of non-COVID-19 related medical equipment have been reported in the documentation available online. 
Furthermore, according to the UNDP report, Paraguay was one of the Latin American countries that best dealt with the health emergency, also due to the low rate of contagion in the country.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: In the available literature, data concerning immigration into the country are reported as discussed in Log n.2570. Instead, there is currently no information available on the emigration from the country since the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic, suggesting that the migratory flow towards the interior of the country probably has prevailed the number of expatriates during the health crisis.
indicator: Migrant workers leaving to work abroad

justification: The government turned to local suppliers to produce sanitize items. Zentiva for instance in a pharmaceutical company based in Czech Republic, produced over 1.5 million hands sanitizers. It was developed, manufactured and supplied to communities within 4 weeks.
indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Waste collection from municipalities have increased during quarantine, as families are forced to stay home. Mixed waste and residual waste collection will increases, however the recycled bio-waste will continue on normally although frequency may reduced.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene
source: Association of Cities and Regions for sustainable Resource management: Czech Republic

source: TFM; Government support schemes for COVID-19

justification: According to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), people's access to prenatal consultations and family planning services in Paraguay has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-April 2020), due to social isolation measures to avoid novel-coronavirus infections. In addition, the medical staff has been reduced, as many health professionals went to confinement for being over 60 years old, and the home visits of community agents were suspended at the beginning of the quarantine. Also, the change of this indicator is also due to behavioral changes, as a large number of pregnant patient have stopped attending prenatal care consultations for fear of contracting the novel-coronavirus in care centers.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: Since the pandemic, humanitarian access has deteriorated. Government lockdown and additional municipalities restrictions restricted NGOs' access to refugee camps, and mobile medical services reaching remote areas and refugee camps had to stop services. Notable NGOs as MSF were able to provide care, but smaller NGOs were particularly impacted, unable to obtain authorisations.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) reported that, during the pandemic, medical staff from non-essential health services was reduced, following the measures to prevent the spread of the coronavirus, and to monitor those who fell into the risk categories of the population (e.g. over 60 years old). Also, home visits of community agents were suspended at the beginning of the quarantine. With the regard to maternal care, a large number of pregnant patient have stopped attending prenatal consultations for fear of contracting the virus in medical centers. To respond to this problem, the Ministry of Health implemented alternative measures to follow the users of these services through virtual platforms and by telephone. The Minister of Health in Paraguay stated that advances such as accompaniment during childbirth by a family member cannot be applied due to the lack of specialized suits. Despite the efforts from the authorities to preserve the provision of non-essential health , the indicator has "decreased" since the beginning of the quarantine.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: Schools had to implement online learning and communications, as well as teaching both teachers and parents how to implement it and how to teach the their children at home
source: Education International; The Impact Of COVID-19 On Czech Education In The Present And Future

The Rosa Women's Centre has experienced a two-fold increase in calls to their help line for domestic violence victims during quarantine
source: Prague civil society Centre: What Covid-19 Taught Us about Domestic Violence

indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification: Due to the dire economic situation, the quality of essential public services was already low before the pandemic, and it has deteriorated considerably since then. Some public sector employees have seen their salaries reduced, hospitals lack beds and equipment, and electricity is less and less available due to the government's inability to pay for fuel oil.
There are no discrimination against minor groups as of yet, however some may arise in future

justification: No sources pertain to a change in alcohol consumption in Syria. It should be noted that alcohol is not banned in Syria as it is for the majority of other Islamic countries, yet no reports indicate an increase or decrease in alcohol consumption.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: WHO and UNICEF has made it their aim/mission to provide children across Syria with vaccines amidst the pandemic. It was a 5-day campaign, implemented by the Syrian Ministry of Health. Health workers checked the vaccination status of more than 900 000 children and vaccinated more than 210 100 children to ensure they are caught up with the routine immunization schedule. WHO states that overall there has been a 5% reduction in vaccine coverage for the first half of 2020. Note that it is uncertain whether the article means that globally vaccine coverage has declined or just in Syria. However, due to this recent campaign it is clear that there is an increased access to vaccines/immunization campaigns in Syria, but it is uncertain whether this campaign would have occurred regardless of the pandemic or not. Given this, the indicator was flagged as an infogap.

No reports or sources specifically states that Syria is experiencing an excess mortality rate. However, this could be due to many COVID-19 cases going unreported in Syria (view alternative source). The first source linked states that with Syria's worrying economic situation, sanctions etc. hospitals are overflowing with COVID-19 patients. As a consequence of this, the source implies that deaths will rise in Syria, attributing to a rise in the mortality rate. However no source specifically states so.

There has been a decreased access to non-essential surgeries in Syria due to fear of COVID-19 infections. The source states that health services have been reduced in hospitals in northwest Syria. It states that: "Initially the local health authorities asked hospitals to temporarily put on hold their outpatient departments (OPD) and non-essential surgeries services." “Since the beginning of the pandemic, there have been occasions when some OPDs had already been closed for weeks in response to alerts or fears about COVID-19.” Prior to the pandemic many doctors have fled Syria due to the war. Therefore, services were already limited. It is uncertain whether there is still limited access to non-essential health services.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: It is uncertain whether COVID-19 has worsen the availability of non-COVID-19 medical supplies, but an article from April states that "Medical supplies are low and at times nonexistent, patients often die of wounds and diseases that are not severe, and medical staff are overworked and often under-qualified." It seems that because Syria's economy was already strained by the war, non-COVID-19 medical supplies were already low in April. It is uncertain whether these conditions still persist and whether supplies are currently still low.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: No reports can be found indicating that health care workers have recently faced violence against them. However, in the past, health care workers and facilities have been attacked. It is stated to be a "Hallmark of the conflict in Syria." Attacks in the past have increased the challenges that healthcare workers in Syria face.

No source gives a statistic for the reported cases in domestic abuse experienced by Syrians. However, one source does state that it has increased (as with other countries). However the number of cases is not available for Syria, because according to the source "In countries like Syria, where the war has not ended and the coronavirus is surging, it is harder to come by real figures." This is because there is often no help for Syrian women due to weak civil society pressures. Therefore, one can assume that abuse often goes unreported, but with the pandemic and worsening economic situations, domestic abuse is likely to increase in Syria.

It is uncertain if an increase in arrests are seen in Syria. According to the source linked, 138 arbitrary arrests were made in April 2020. This is not uncommon. Since the conflict in Syria of 2011, arbitrary arrests and forced disappearances have been common. No reports state that an increase in arrests were made since the pandemic. Fear over COVID-19 spread in the prisons have sparked riots in the prisons (view alternative source), but no mention of COVID-19 attributing to arrests.

According to the source linked, Unicef has warned that the pandemic has set back efforts to reduce child labour among refugee children in Syria by a decade. It therefore implies that child labour is increasing amongst Syrians to help provide for families suffering from economic hardships. The specific number of increases is not found in any source, however the sources linked do imply that the numbers have increased.

Eight Syrian armed non-State actors (ANSAs) are active in Syria. The non-state actors have signed a “Unilateral Declaration on COVID-19 and Health Care” supported by Geneva Call to safeguard access to health care and help preventing the spread of COVID-19. It is therefore undetermined what level of authority they impose. It would seem that their interest in signing the declaration implies that they want to “respect and protect health care personnel, transports, facilities and goods”, to “take preventive measures to avoid COVID-19 spreading that are necessary and proportionate to protect public health” and to “ensure, maintain and provide access for affected populations to essential health care facilities, goods and services without discrimination” and “facilitate the provision of health care by impartial humanitarian organizations”. It is uncertain what level of authority they have.

It was found that child marriages in will "spike" in Syria due to the COVID-19 impact. Many drivers add an increase to this indicator including conflict, displacement, poverty, and social and cultural pressures. Therefore behavioural changes also have an influence. As COVID-19 continues to push Syrians into poverty, child marriages will continue to increase. The alternative source states that increasing number of Syrian refugee girls are being married of to Turkish men in Turkey to ease financial barriers caused by COVID-19.

No relevant sources could be found pertaining to changing patterns of human trafficking in Syria. Only one recent article was found, but does not mention increasing or decreasing instances of trafficking in Syria.

Change in this indicator was labelled as 'increased' since the elections held in 2020 in Syria were supposed to be held in April but were postponed. When viewing the alternative source, one can see that the elections took place in July.
indicator: Elections taking place as scheduled pre-COVID

justification: Protests in the Syrian capital have cited to be 'rare', but seems to have increased amidst effects that COVID-19 had on the war-torn country. The pandemic, U.S. sanctions and the Lebanon economic crisis seem to have worsened the economic crisis in Syria. All of this has resulted in compounding effects resulting in the protests at the capital. Protestors began with economic demands but soon clashed with supporters of Iran-backed Hezbollah calling for the downfall of the Assad government. Overall, the pandemic "wiped out" the little income which some Syrians still had. All of these factors explain the protests that have broke out in Syria as it is directly related to COVID-19. It should be known that the article does not report when this year did the protests occur, but the source date is in September.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: Protests unrelated to COVID-19 have occurred in city of Sweida on June 15. Civilians have protested because of deteriorating living conditions and corruption in Syria following the deteriorating economy and collapsing currency. Civilians are struggling to feed their children as protests arose due to soaring food prices. It is undetermined whether a change in the number of protests are seen. Considering that the economic crises started a few months ago one can infer that protests have increased during the last few months, yet this is uncertain. Considering Syria always had economic difficulties ever since the war broke out in 2011, it is difficult to determine whether protests only recently rose. This indicator was therefore labelled as an infogap.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification:
It is uncertain whether access to sexual and reproductive services have changed amidst the pandemic. It would not seem that access declined due to COVID-19 restriction, but access to such services were already limited due to the effects that the 9 years of war had on the health care system. The report states that "only 2 of 11 hospitals are fully functioning and that no district in northeast Syria meets the minimum emergency threshold of at least 10 beds for every 10,000 people, while just 1 district has enough doctors, nurses, and midwives to meet the minimum emergency threshold of at least 22 health care workers for every 10,000 people." It is obvious that access to such services are limited, however the cause of  the limited access is attributed to the war and not COVID-19. In the alternative source one can see that health partners in Syria have conducted a second round of COVID-19 IPC training. It targets
workers in specialised health centres, such as those providing maternal, newborn and child health services. It would therefore seem that preparation for the pandemic has helped northwest Syria. This would allow for greater access to sexual and reproductive services. However, whether these services have indeed increased, especially considering the war-torn state of the country, is difficult to determine.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: More than 6 million internally displaced Syrians and other vulnerable groups remain inside Syria. However, whether or not the number of IDPs in Syria have increased/decreased because of the pandemic is unknown as no sources specifically state so. Many sources imply that the vulnerabilities that internally displaced Syrians often have are increasing because of the pandemic. For example the UNHCR had seen: “another 200,000 refugees just in this period of three months, who because of the impact, needed emergency assistance”. This indicator is flagged as an infogap because no sources have stated that the number of IDPs have changed because of the pandemic.
indicator: Internal Displacement and Mobility related to COVID-19

justification: All sources relate to discrimination and violence faced by Syrian refugees in host countries. No sources were found pertaining to discrimination or violence within Syria itself. Therefore, this indicator has an infogap. The discrimination and violence occurring in host countries are as follow. Movement restrictions are specifically being targeted onto Syrian refugees in host countries such as Lebanon. Syrians in Lebanon are facing challenges as certain municipalities are implementing restrictions on movement specifically targeted at refugees. These policies puts Syrians in Lebanon at increased risk and causes anti-refugee sentiment and xenophobia. Furthermore, the leader of Lebanon’s Forces Party, Samir Geagea stated that “full measures must be taken in the vicinity of the Palestinian and Syrian refugee camps and to prevent entry and exit to them” The source states that this authoritative figure is implying that refugees are a potential source of the spread of COVID-19 rather than potential victims. Restrictions include that Syrians are only allowed to move around the municipality between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. where only necessary tasks are allowed. These curfews are said to be stricter than the nationwide lockdown. Syrian refugees (marginalized groups) are facing increased discrimination from authorities of host countries, such as Lebanon.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups
source: The Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC)

justification: The marginalised groups in Syria include the refugees and IDPs. From this group, women, children and old people are even more vulnerable and marginalised (see alternative source). The journal article linked states that it is usually the refugees who have limited access to medical help. Furthermore, lack of preventative measures such as screening and COVID-19 tests cause these refugees to become more vulnerable.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: No sources provide information on stigmatisation or hostile language used against refugees by authorities within Syria.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification: Sources state that authorities of other countries where Syrian refugees reside have abused human rights. For example, in March, Jordan announced it would not allow relief aid to pass through its territory to deliver assistance and medical equipment to a Syrian refugee camp, due to COVID-19 concerns. It is obvious that this is a form of abuse against the vulnerable refugees in Syria. However, this was flagged as an infogap as no sources pertain to Syrian authorities abusing human rights of refugees.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: Inflation (overall) has increased in Syria due to a number of reasons. Ramadan caused an increase in this year's inflation. This is because prices always increase on a year-to-year basis during Ramadan. Secondly the war, which has greatly affected shipping and imports; and lastly COVID-19, which has shut down parts of the supply chain. In the month of May, food prices increased by 25% alone. No source could be found for an increase in the monthly inflation rate specifically. However, it is safe to assume that as food inflation, and other inflations are seen in the country, the monthly inflation is certainly increasing.

No movement restrictions have been imposed in Syria to effect the economy itself, but the economic crises it has caused globally is affecting the humanitarian needs of the more than 11 million people across Syria. This source now states that 90% of Syrians are in poverty. Unemployment is also high and is further affected by COVID-19 restrictions in Syria. The alternative source states that basic foods and other needs are unaffordable in Syria.

Remittances sent to Syria is stated to be a "vital economic lifeline to Syria". Remittances have slowed down/declined that is received in Syria due to the global economic slow down caused by COVID-19. The source also states that "without a dependable supply of foreign currency reserves, the Central Bank of Syria will struggle to finance imports." It should be noted that COVID-19 has not significantly changed Syria but it highlighted the economic strain that the country was already in and accelerated the economic deterioration. It should also be noted that evidence shows that remittances to Syria were already declining prior to the pandemic.
source: Center for Operational Analysis and Research (COAR)

justification: 95% of Syrian refugees within Jordan and Lebanon have reported a decrease in their household disposable income. Although this is not for people within in Syria itself, COVID-19 still conveys an effect on the many Syrians outside of Syria. The decline in household disposable income is due to lockdown measures imposed in the host countries (Jordan and Lebanon). Note that no source date was provided.

COVID-19 has said to have caused increasing costs of staple foods in Syria. The source states that: "The cost of a representative basket of staple foods has doubled in just over six months, according to the UN’s food aid agency." This is attributed to the declining currency in Syria and the fact that COVID-19 has disrupted food chains.
With closures of schools, the World Food Programme explicitly stated that it has suspended the programme due to the closures of schools. This will effect more than 1 million children in Syria.
No information can be found pertaining to a change in Syria's net primary school enrollment rate.

According to the report linked, different COVID-19 measures were imposed on northeast and northwestern Syria. Vendors in the northeastern area reported from a survey conducted that only essential stores are open. Nonetheless, this implies that there is access to essential goods. In the northwestern part of Syria, vendors reported that no preventative measures have been implemented by authorities. 72% of the vendors adopted their own measures (using gloves in their shops). Nonetheless, it would seem that their shops/markets are also open. Therefore, there is no change in the access to markets in Syria.

Access to higher education facilities have decreased as universities and schools closed in mid-march (view alternative source). When viewing the first source linked, Universities lack online learning sources. Therefore, access to higher educational facilities and resources have definitely decreased. It should be noted that the alternative source states that Universities and Schools are preparing to reopen.

Syria is experiencing a decreasing food security (as shown in Q3) or increasing food insecurity. This is because of “Years of war, mismanagement, oppression, now exacerbated by the economic crisis in neighbouring Lebanon, have aggravated the economic crisis in Syria.” It is clear that the Syrian government plays a role due to mismanagement (governmental drive). Furthermore, COVID-19 can worsen this due to disruption in commercial supply chains. Food insecurity is said to have continuing rising in Syria as it can soon exceed 11 million people.

The Syrian government decided to end the school year in mid-March.  Online learning was broadcasted on education TV channels as well as other online teaching methods. However, many challenges persist for online learning. Therefore, a decreased access to education facilities occurred due to COVID-19. As seen in the alternative source, it should be noted that schools are preparing to re-open.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

justification: No sources report statistics on Syrian migrants leaving Syria to work abroad as most Syrians are classified as refugees. This presents confusion in finding an accurate statistic and relevant sources.
indicator: Migrant workers leaving to work abroad

justification: No sources report statistics on Syrian migrants returning to Syria from abroad as most Syrians are classified as refugees. This presents confusion in finding an accurate statistic and relevant sources.

Humanitarian aid provided (mostly by international actors) have been restricted by the Syrian government (even prior to COVID-19) because of the aid being received in opposition-controlled areas. This forms part of the government's efforts to regain control of the entire country. It would seem that the change and potential decreasing availability of aid provided to those in need are increasingly being influenced by governmental measures/restrictions for political reasons. However, on top of political unrest imposing movement restrictions to humanitarian access, COVID-19 has added to the restriction. The spread of Covid-19 has said to curtail NGO activities in the area by hindering their attempts to lead the pandemic response and delivering humanitarian aid. The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) restricted movement across the Faysh Khabour crossing to guard against the spread of the disease, and NGOs are only able to cross once a week. There is therefore a decreased access to humanitarian aid to those in need because of political restrictions and restrictions implemented caused by the pandemic.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: The only relevant source found states that "public services have collapsed" in Syria. This is not enough to derive conclusions from and is therefore and infogap.

It is uncertain what the impact of COVID-19 is on international aid and this indicator was therefore flagged as an infogap. However, it seems that there are no cut backs in the aid provided to Syria when considering the first article linked. The article states that International communities have pledged US$5.5 billion for the Syria crisis response in 2020. The money is given to the UN to help in their aid response to Syria. Furthermore, the alternative source states that training of laboratory technicians are ongoing in Syria and equipment had been shipped to set up laboratories in Aleppo, Lattakia and Homs. Moreover, "WHO’s further broad response includes supporting active surveillance planning inclusive of north-east Syria, and specialized technical and information trainings." It would therefore seem that international aid is not being suspended or cut in Syria.

It is uncertain if local NGO aid has been cut or suspended in Syria. The first source linked states that a local NGO Al-Bir and Al-Ihsan in Syria were unable to operate their mobile health clinics in Aleppo due to travel bans between urban and rural areas. Although this example does not state that the program itself is suspending cuts, it emphasises how restrictions imposed by the government can influence decisions made on programs and their ability to provide aid. The second source linked further emphasises how the Syrian government has placed restrictions on International aid, which could certainly influence local NGOs as well.
No sources state that public services are becoming privatized in Syria.

It is difficult to determine if there is a change in access for Syrians to humanitarian aid as a result of restrictions caused by COVID-19. According to the article linked there is a great need for humanitarian assistance in refugee camps. The source states that: "As MSF we are trying to meet as many of people’s needs as we can and to support the work of other organisations. But, far more attention and commitments are needed; areas such as the Annex have all but been abandoned by the world." Restriction in access to humanitarian aid is often driven by the conflict in Syria. It is therefore difficult to determine from sources if COVID-19 has caused decreased access or if it was already decreased due to the conflict. Organisations such as the Medicins Sans Frontiers (MSF) have provided training at a hospital in the northeast Syria region as part of the COVID-19 humanitarian taskforce. However at other times humanitarian aid had to be withdrawn due to the conflict. This indicator was flagged as an infogap as sources do not specifically state that Syrian refugees have a decreased access to humanitarian aid due to COVID-19 restrictions, but rather that there is an increasing need for aid. Furthermore, aid is often restricted by conflict as noted in the source.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification:
The only source of evidence relating to a change in the consumption of alcohol was a small survey conducted amongst Israeli university students. This indicator was therefore left as an infogap as it does not apply to the whole of the Israeli population. The questionnaire was conducted between 170 Israeli- and 121 Russian university students where their consumption of alcohol and other substance use was questioned. The survey found that respondents who used substances prior to the
COVID-19 reported more than usual use during the governmental lockdown regulations (quarantine and social distancing period).
The percentage of substance users reporting COVID-19-related increase is cigarettes (43.7%);
alcohol (38.9%); and cannabis (52.5%). Therefore the use of these substances have increased in relation to the COVID-19 mental health effects. Furthermore, open-ended questions of the survey showed answers such as: “I drink wine more often than usual due to being at home more than the usual…”;
“I began to drink often on weekends to forget …”; “I smoke cigarettes because I’m at home
more, feel the need for a release and to compensate for other hardships that I’m dealing with…"
The survey therefore shows that students increased their substance use during the COVID-19 pandemic.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

The impact of COVID-19 on some public services in Paraguay has caused interruptions or suspensions of the service to citizens. Since June 24, the Supreme Court of Justice suspended the activities of the judicial power in different judicial districts, including the capital. Since the beginning of May, The Central Bank of Paraguay implemented new measures adopted by the government to limit the attendance of the public to its facilities as much as possible. On July 20, authorities suggested foreigners to start their temporary and permanent settlement procedures from abroad. 
On the other hand, some other public services such as those regarding the security and public health, have been significantly strengthened in the face of the pandemic. On April 10, the Government enacted the supervision of the isolation for those who have tested positive for coronavirus. Since middle July 2020, there has been a further increase in epidemiological surveillance and preventive isolation management. The change in this indicator was classified as undetermined.
