Remittances are a vital source of income for many of the poorest households accounting for 15% of the GDP and are projected to plunge by more than 50%, worsening hardship for the poorest households. The decrease in personal remittances is also impacted by behavioural change such as the sudden shift in attitudes, wanting to be with family and also out of fear of staying in the host country during unprecedented times.

All schools in Uzbekistan have been closed since the 15th of March and the new academic year is yet to commence in september after an extended summer break due to the uncertainties surrounding the pandemic.

The unprecedented lockdown meant that universities and higher education institutes had to close and switch to remote learning. The issue of equity meant not all students have the same access to higher education facilities. The crisis has disproportionately hit the most vulnerable households. Students living in remote areas do not have consistent access to electronic devices or the internet.

All primary and secondary schools have transitioned to virtual remote forms of learning for 6.1 million students. The government has released over 350 videos on national TV channels available in Uzbek, Russian and Sign language. Lessons are also available on Youtube and other in-house learning platforms. However many of these emergency educational tools are aimed at grade 1-11 students excluding other years. Furthemore one- third of the population does not have internet access and 50% of the population lives in rural areas. This highlights the issues of equity as not all students equal access to distance learning resources and opportunities when schools are shut down.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

justification: The government has made lessons available for grade 1-11 students on national TV channels and Youtube. To supplement learning the ministry has granted free data access to make resources accessible for all students. University examinations have been postponed to September and are taking place in stadiums and open air spaces. Students are required to wear masks and gloves which are provided by the examination board and students are spaced 3 meters apart for additional protection.

In Paraguay, the United Nations has supported the National Government in the fight against COVID-19 since the beginning of the pandemic. In particular, the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) has launched, together with the SDG Commission, UN agencies and civil society organizations, a national crowdfunding campaign called “All for Paraguay”, which is intended to raise funds to supplement efforts. of the State in the fight against the pandemic. All proceeds will go to biomedical equipment and personal protective supplies, as well as lung ventilators, multi-paramedic monitors, anesthesia machines, alcohol, face masks and face masks. The measures adopted, both economic and health, are accompanied by the multilateral organizations residing in Paraguay that encourage all sectors to join forces to achieve an effective fight against the virus and reduce the harmful effects of this health crisis.

The commitment of local Non-Governmental Organizations was significant during the pandemic especially in protecting the human rights of indigenous communities, which suffered discrimination by the Government, not receiving the necessary health aid and social protection from the authorities. The role of NGOs in this aim was to denounce the authorities asking for more support for the most vulnerable populations in a health emergency situation.
source: Consejo de Educación Popular de América Latina y el Caribe (CEAAL)

Combined with reduced urban demand and oversupply, producer prices are rapidly declining. justification:
Research shows that the uncertainty, the disease itself, fake news, isolation, the population's misunderstanding of health messages and the prohibition of travelling increased cases of mental disorders, such as anxiety and depressive disorders and PTSD. The newspaper The Arab Weekly reported a spike in suicides and suicide attempts since the pandemic, mainly due to the deterioration of economic conditions. Men are the most concerned. "From January 1 to July 30, 2020, males accounted for 165 of the cases and females for 128."

Yazidis displaced in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, who escaped from ISIS, already have several traumas and mental health issues and the pandemic poses more risks. The lockdown and restrictions of movement prevented the few psychologists already present from visiting their patients. According to the findings of Kizilhan and Noll-Hussong, who analysed the effects of COVID-19 on the mental health in a refugee camp in Iraq, “the probability of PTSD and other mental disorders in refugees, especially females, increased”. The isolation, disinformation, uncertainty, loss of control, restriction on movement, lack of access to medical care, the fear of losing loved ones and getting sick “probably reactivated the traumatic experience with a feeling of helplessness, similar to that during captivity or flight.”

justification: Self-employed workers selling food on wheelcarts (called carretilleros) to neighbourhoods have had licenses revoked by the state, meaning that families have been left with no choice but to go to state-owned markets, which has paradoxically exacerbated scarcity.

The words were conveyed by the media and have been left open to interpretation, leading shops to refuse to serve customers with visible disabilities

source: Granma - Official Voice of the Communist Party of Cuba Central Committee

justification: The pandemic caused severe disruptions to polio campaigns across the country. It left 50 million children without access to the vaccination. However vaccinations have restarted since August. Door to door vaccinations have been suspended with only healthcare clinic vaccinations.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Honduras experienced an increase of more than 10 percentage points in the share of people facing acute hunger since the beginning of the pandemic (March-July 2020), as a result of the contingency measures that indirectly limited access to markets and cross-border trade. Moreover, as reported by OCHA, increased staple food prices contribute negatively to the change of this indicator; the driver of this impact is therefore classified as "Governmental Measures" and the food security of the country's population has been logged as "decreased" since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) retrieved through ReliefWeb

justification:
According to OCHA, the pandemic "has exacerbated already insufficient access
to potable/safe water and inadequate sanitation services specially to
conflict-affected people in many districts."  
The rehabilitation of water treatment facilities has been put on hold due to movement restriction, which increases the risk of getting ill (COVID-19, cholera...). Health care, internally displaced people, informal settlements and some cities as Basra are particularly affected.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification: Movement restriction measures greatly impacted small and medium enterprises, which had to close or reduce working hours and employee numbers. Consequently, several workers have seen their wages reduced. However, few employees were laid off. The hospitality sector is  the most affected in terms of expected job losses, and the oil sector had to lay off many employee as the pandemic engendered a fall in oil prices.

The informal sector, which employs more than 50% of the workforce, is affected by a great level of unemployment and young workers are the most impacted. 
Informal workers are not protected and do not benefit from social protection schemes for workers, leading to financial difficulties.
No information on provision of public services as of yet.

justification: For the month of April, the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs established the Minha programme, a one-time financial relief package to people economically affected by movement restrictions. Around 11.6 million Iraqi will receive 30 000 IQD (25 USD).
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

justification: There has been calls by an umbrella NGO organisation-VENRO-for the German government to consider providing more financial funds and aid/support to INGOs within the umbrella during COVID 19. There is however no information available on the impact of COVID 19 on INGO scheduled programmes and reduced staff numbers.
It has been reported that NGOs in Germany, without government financial support, would expect cuts to programmes.

Inflation slightly hit Iraq in January but increased in February and March. However, this indicator is logged as an info-gap as the impact of the pandemic on prices is not clear. Price control measures helped to reduce inflation and maintain a low level, despite a small increase in May (from 0.2% in February to 0.7% in May).
There is an info-gap for this indicator. However, according to UNICEF, losses of jobs and inflation will contribute to an increase in the poverty rate.
Although there is no information on the changes to household disposable income, it is safe to say that it has decreased due to job losses.

Border closures and domestic mobility restrictions are likely to have caused disruptions. However, since no reports describing disruptions to humanitarian activities could be found, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

Forecasts suggest that Cuba's unemployment rate will hit 3% by the end of 2020. However, the real unemployment rate is reportedly much higher (37.7%). Since information on changes per se could not be found, this indicator has  been marked with an InfoGap.

President Donald Trump announced new restrictions on remittances to Cuba in June 2020. It is expected that this will have an impact on remittances received, but no information confirming this could be found. The Cuban government does not publish remittance figures either, so this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

No reports could be found indicating any changes in human trafficking. Therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

Despite the non-disclosure of statistics related to domestic violence, activists have stated that the number of incidents and the number of people requiring support has grown in the wake of the pandemic.
The Ministry of Public Health outlined plans to gradually restore various non-COVID-19 related treatments such as rehabilitation, after being disrupted since the pandemic began.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: The French government changed the labour laws in March to account for wider changes brought in to stem the spread of COVID-19. Employers can make employees take holiday with just one day's notice (max 10 days) and can suspend the right for partners to take holiday at the same time. Employers can also modify the working hours of the employee without their agreement. For necessary industries, such as security and economy, the working day has increased by 2 hours and the working week has increased from 48 to 60 hours.
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections
source: Ministry of Work, Employment and Integration

justification: Inflation decreased slightly in September compared to August due to a slowing down in prices of services and energy. The prices of manufactured goods slowed at the same rate in August and the price of food increased at the same rate as in August.
source: National Institute for Statistics and Economic Studies

justification: A widely cited report published by the charity Secours Populaire observes that in the two months of lockdown (mid-March to mid-April) 1,270,000 people used their services. This compares to 3,268,460 users in  all of 2019. Furthermore, 45% of the service users were new to the charity. The precarious situation created by the health crisis is understood to be the driver of the increase particularly for old people, single-parent families and poor workers.

Compared to the previous quarter, the household disposable income has decreased by the largest percentage since 1949. Household income is down by 7.6% compared to the previous quarter but this large decrease was cushioned somewhat by an increase of 5.6% in social benefits.  This has been due to the decrease in employment and the decrease in working hours permitted by the government.
source: National Institute for Statistics and Economic Studies

justification: No information available relating to personal remittances in Iraq could be found.

There is a lack of data regarding the specific COVID-19 relationship. However, the amount of direct capital invested by French people abroad has increased from 0.25 billion in May to 0.3 billion in July. This is a significant decrease compared to May 2019 which saw the direct investment of 11.4 billion euros.

There has been a decrease in enrolment but this was predicted due to the smaller cohort in the population. The government made returning to school mandatory except in cases justified by medical certification.
source: Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport

justification: No information available relating to changes to the national rate of enrolment in primary schools.

Access to universities was first disrupted by the protest calling the end of the corrupted system, and then the pandemic. Most universities across the country provided online lectures and exams were rescheduled and held online. But some challenges remain: not all students have internet access and not all the universities have enough budget, a strong internet connexion, and a good ICT infrastructure.

Primary and secondary schools have been closed since February affecting 10 million children and reopened in May only to allow students to take their mid-term exams, delayed due to national protests. 
Where funds and infrastructures were available, schools provided remote learning. 
The Ministry of Education in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq in coordination with UNESCO and UNICEF, provided remote learning (e-learning and a satellite TV channel) to IDPs, returnees and refugees, during schools closure. However, in Iraq, many families do not have the equipment and internet connection needed. 
The Ministry of Education also distributed sterilized material to allow students to attend the exam session safely.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

justification:
Prior to the pandemic, universities already started to implement remote learning programmes as student deserted classrooms to lead protests. These programmes then continued to expand.
Remote learning and a satellite TV channel for education in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq were also implemented for primary and secondary schools. 
However, not all institutions have the funding, a reliable internet connection and infrastructures to efficiently provide online learning programmes.

Associations recorded a spike in domestic violence against women and children cases during the curfew and hotlines were overwhelmed. The head of Iraq's community police told AFP that during the first weeks of the lockdown, "domestic violence cases has increased by an average of 30 percent since the curfew came into force -- with some areas seeing as high as a 50-percent spike."
In August, the government, pressured by NGOs and the population, submitted to the parliament two draft domestic violence bills. They would be the first, as no legislation exists on domestic violence in the Iraqi penal code.

Access to sexual and reproductive health services was already limited as several wars partially destruct hospitals. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the access became more limited due to the closure of some of the health centres, movement restriction measures and the fear of getting sick. This fear is all the more important as a woman who catches the virus is stigmatised and may never find a husband. In addition, health centres are running out of contraceptive pills.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: Mental health cases have risen in Afghanistan primarily due to the fear and anxieties surrounding the pandemic. There has been an increase in the rate of suicides and anxiety faced by the population. Suicide rates have been high among young Afghans who have faced significant feelings of extreme hopelessness specifically among those groups of individuals fleeing from Iran back to Afghanistan in an attempt to avoid the COVID-19 hotspot.

Organisations such as the WFP have reported their assistance figures, and no reports could be found indicating that there has been a disruption in humanitarian access to people in need. Nevertheless, border closures mean that humanitarian aid workers may have been prevented from entering the country - therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: The elimination of tax on USD has facilitated the use of the currency to purchase goods. However, in tandem with growing scarcity and buying/selling in the informal market, there are increasing levels of inflation.
Fears of COVID-19 transmission in prisons led authorities to parole 6579 prisoners and release 412 detainees as of 1 May 2020.

Recent reports indicate that Cuba has imposed restrictions banning the consumption of alcohol in public spaces but no information could be found regarding possible changes in consumption or abuse rates. Therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

justification: Border closures and domestic mobility restrictions are likely to have caused disruptions, and have contributed to Oxfam's decision to close down its country office (no withdrawal date confirmed).

Cuba does not have any scheduled elections for 2020. Therefore, this indicator has been marked as Not Applicable.
indicator: Voter turnout in latest national elections that took place since beginning of covid pandemic

justification: Whilst the time period of the incurred costs could not be verified, reports indicate that 125 million pesos were spent in costs related to COVID-19, such as food provision to those self-isolating, as well as welfare payments amongst other things in Havana. It is possible that increased spending was seen in other regions but in the absence of reports, this indicator has been marked as having a Localised Geographic Impact.

Water supply problems have been acknowledged by Cuban authorities and reportedly intend to accelerate infrastructure projects. However, as changes could not be verified, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

Alcohol and substance consumption is forbidden in Afghanistan due to religious reasons. Those who do indulge do so very privately due to the taboo connotations surrounding its consumption. Thus, this is considered an infogap.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: The pandemic has had a negative impact on food security. The price of staple foods have significantly increased, increasing the overall number of food insecure people in the country to 31 million. Ongoing conflict, widespread unemployment and food price hikes  resulting from the pandemic have contributed to the widespread level of food insecurity.

Staple food prices have increased by 10-20% across the country. This has been linked to border closures and panic buying which has further pushed households below the poverty line. Import restrictions has meant that there is a wheat and flour shortage, the limited supply will also affect future food prices.

Border closures with Pakistan and Iran have affected the main supply routes for critical items such as rice and flour. Kazakhstan being an important supplier of wheat and wheat flour to Afghanistan has also imposed restrictions that has  resulted in an abrupt price hike of wheat, flour and oil.
indicator: Ability of international food supply chain to support domestic food availability

justification: Disruption to internal travel routes have caused disruptions across the country leaving farmers with a lot of stock in some areas and a scarcity in urban areas also resulting in inflation.

Many Afghans work as daily labourers, and with cities like Herat and Kabul going into lockdown  and the possibility that other urban centres will follow,  this means that many people have to choose between staying home  hungry or venturing outside to find work. Increased transport fares for going into the city has also deterred many wage workers from working thus significantly reducing the workforce.
The pandemic has impacted this indicator but there is not available data so this is logged as an infogap.

On 16th March, all educational establishments closed and moved to online learning to stem the spread of the COVID-19. On the 12th April schools started to re-open in areas with a low number of cases and there was some flexibility abut whether to re-enrol one's child or not. From 22nd June, it was compulsory for all children to be attending school unless they had a medical justification. Some schools have been closed temporarily due to Covid infections. Currently 14 are closed compared to 19 last week and 89 the week before.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

justification: Universities were closed in March and only re-opened in September to stem the spread of COVID-19. Students returned to in person learning with masks and social distancing. Some universities, such as Université Lumière Lyon 2, have implemented a staggered return focusing initially on the first years. Currently universities in certain regions are closed for two weeks for example in Compiègne. On the 30th September, the Minister of Universities rejected a blanket closure after a third of clusters were found in educational environments.

When schools closed on 16th March to stem the spread of COVID-19, remote learning was implemented across the country and across educational levels. Universities were better able to cope with the change compared to primary schools which had little online learning capacity at the time. Since the schools went back in April, universities have been the only educational establishment to continue with online learning full-time until September. Online learning tools are still available for those unable to attend in person learning but most teaching and learning is now being done in person.
source: Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport

justification: There is no sufficient information on a change in the availability of non-COVID-19 medical supplies in Nigeria. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: France does not have any non-state armed groups. There was a small armed separatist group in Corsica but this disbanded in 2016. Some reports of very small clusters of separatist violence i 2017 but nothing since then and no group officially claiming it.

France does not collect official statistics on CEFM. It had conducted surveys to find out information. In 2013, 70,000 women were at risk of CEFM. In 2014, it was reported that 4% of immigrant and 2% of daughters of immigrants had experienced CEFM.

The number of calls to the national domestic violence helpline significantly increased during the national lockdown (mid-March to mid-April).  Lockdown is said to have been a trigger for domestic violence. In April there were three times more calls than in February. In all of 2019, there were 90,000 calls, whilst in March, April and May 2020 there were 44,235. There has been a 46% increase in the number of police interventions in the home due to family problems. This is partly due to the Minister of the Interior's recent focus on increasing home interventions.
source: Ministry for Gender Equality, Diversity and Equality of Opportunities

justification: There have been numerous reports of widespread shortages of PPE and Hygiene items in particular hand gel. In response to these reports, the Minister of Health decided to establish an export restriction for protective clothing to prevent outright shortages of PPE for Germany in March. There have been reports of empty pharmacy shelves and  price hikes due to increased demand by third party sellers from German Pharmaceutical Production Companies

indicator: Internal Displacement and Mobility related to COVID-19

justification: Germany has experienced low levels of excess mortality rate even amongst the most vulnerable population of ages 65+. The government also allowed past prescriptions for the contraceptive pill to be used in pharmacies to get a repeat prescription.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: Ethnic minorities were disproportionately targeted by the police in interventions monitoring the compliance of lockdown (mid-March to mid-May) regulations. Fears of violence against the LGBTQ+ community saw the launch of the FLAG! app supported by the Minister of the Interior to report incidences of homophobia. One of the proposed lockdown exit strategies which was rejected would have prejudiced the elderly in their limitations of movement.

justification:
Child labour is a dire issue in Iraq, and the pandemic increased the need for families to send their children to work. With the lockdown, unemployment rose and schools were closed, forcing more children to help their family to make ends meet. 
Kurdish families, internally displaced persons and Syrian refugees children are the most vulnerable.

There is little information of France specifically. There is a lot on the global increase and the risk of many falling prey to exploitation and trafficking due to reduced livelihoods and desperation. In France, a trend of exploitation identified was young people exchanging their asylum seeker identity cards for small amounts of cash. This was often the beginning of other forms of exploitation.

The vulnerable population in Iraq, IDPs, returnees, refugees and those leaving in remote and conflict-affected areas, have less access to health care facilities due to movement restriction measures. Sometimes, the nearest hospital is several kilometres away, and checkpoints prevent access to cities. 
WHO deployed mobile clinics to reach the most vulnerable population.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: No information relating to changes in the number of incarcerations could be found.

Although several defeats weakened ISIS, the terrorist group benefit from the COVID-19 chaos to increase attacks in Iraq. ISIS is mainly operating in rural areas and before the pandemic, Iraqi security forces were deployed to fight the group. Since March, the government redeployed them in urban areas to monitor the lockdown, easing the pressure on ISIS. Moreover, the reallocation of soldiers engendered the suspension of military operations against ISIS. Yet, the weakness of Iraqi forces does not only date back to the COVID-19 pandemic, and tension amid factions and the lack of coordination and equipment have been hindering their efficiency.
ISIS also uses the pandemic as propaganda, asserting that it supports their discourse, as it is impacting the US and Western Europe more than Iraq.

Recent data on the numbers of children in work could not be found but France has joined an alliance called Alliance 8.7, along with UNICEF and ILO, aimed at decreasing child labour by making certain social and political changes. France has expressed a wish to be a pioneering country in this area so political changes are expected.
source: Ministry of European and Foreign Affairs

justification:
Violence against health workers is not new in Iraq, but with the rise of the number of cases during summer, verbal and physical violence has soared. 
In rural and conservative areas, the population, who distrust the government, do not believe in the disease and think it is a hoax and a political conspiracy. Thus, they refuse, often violently, to be tested. Health workers are also held responsible for the death of a relative and the scarcity of medical equipment and can be threatened if they try to report a case to the authorities (as the community might stigmatise the family). The most affected governorates are Thi Qar, Basra, and Baghdad.

In Baghdad, Health worker protested in September to ask the government to take action and protect them against the rise of violent assaults against them during the pandemic. 
In the Kurdish region, the population manifested against a new lockdown implemented in June, claiming that economic opportunities are already scarce and lockdowns worsen the situation.  Under pressure, the government lifted the lockdown after one day.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification:
Despite the curfew and lockdown, some Iraqi occupied Tahrir square and many other places across the country, to protest the corrupted elite and ask for better economic opportunities. Brutal repression against protesters continued, and several clashes, arrests and deaths were reported. 
Health workers protest for more security and jobs. Many Iraqi are graduates from medical schools, while the country counts one of the lowest numbers of doctors and nurses per capita in the MENA region.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification: A report by Insée found that the numbers of deaths of immigrants rose twice as high as those born in France during the COVID-19 health crisis. The reaction to this report is a hope that France will pay greater attention to long neglected communities.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support
source: National Institute for Statistics and Economic Studies

justification: Many small businesses have reported restrictions in procuring  fresh agricultural produce and difficulties in transporting produce to local markets due to increased transportation costs  and road closures. Over half of markets were reported as functioning as usual. 40% of vegetable markets have been adversely affected and only 50% of street vendors are operating as usual.

Afghanistan already faces inadequate health facilities and a lack of basic services including access to clean water and sanitation. Those daily challenges have been magnified by the spread of covid-19 and the economic implications of the lockdown. The cost of basic essentials have increased dramatically. Women and girls are struggling to access sanitary items during the lockdown due to their limited access to markets.
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Decreased availability of sanitation items due to increased cost and access to markets due to travel restrictions and scarcity across the country.
indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: The pandemic has affected the WASH sector especially in terms of disruption of funding. However in most COVID-19 risk areas, including informal settlements, the basic WASH services have been improved and are accompanied by key specific transmission mitigation measures which are closely measured. This includes physical distancing when queuing at collective water points or at hygiene kit distribution centres, hygiene sessions and focus group discussions.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification: No reports on interrupted domestic food supply chains

There is no solid evidence change in people's access to markets. There are scattered cases of people going less to the market due to containment measures and behavioural changes (e.g. fear to get infected). Some establishments have also been closed due to staff tested positive for COVID-19.

Other people have had initiatives to grow foods and communicate via new online platforms, reinventing domestic agricultural production and facilitating producer to consumer sales for organic products. Initiatives to build urban vegetable gardens in the cities to avoid food shortages have also been promoted. Similar food reserves have been established in some Indigenous communities to face the pandemic.
No reports on interrupted domestic food supply chains.
indicator: Domestic food supply chain (available labour force)

justification: Since March, the government has established a programme to cover the students who were formerly attending school feeding schemes (the PANEA, Programa de Alimentación y Nutrición del Escolar y del Adolescente). Official data reports a great coverage (almost 100% of the students that attendended school feeding programmes prior to the pandemic).

The FAO showed data that revelead a general increase in food prices in February/March in different countries of Latin America, including Costa Rica. The official monthly measure of the cost of staple foods (in Costa Rica: "canasta básica alimentaria", CBA) has also shown a relatively slight increase in the last months according to the INEC (National Institute of Statistics), with the exception of the transition from April to May. This could be attributed to increased costs of production, greater difficulties for import, etc.  Moreover, in July the CBA (basic staple foods) started to be taxed with 1% (VAT), and other products stopped being part of the CBA and were taxed with the normal VAT (13%), to which some consumers and ministers have shown opposition.

According to a study of CCS (Cámara de Comercio de Santiago), Costa Rica was the 2nd country in employment loss in the world between March and June (with a 21% employment loss).

justification: The latest Gambian national election was held in April 2017. Therefore, no elections have taken place during the pandemic, making this indicator not applicable. There is no available source date.
indicator: Voter turnout in latest national elections that took place since beginning of covid pandemic

justification:
There are no relevant information regarding a change in 
stigmatisation against a specific group in Gambia with relevancy to the pandemic. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification: The next national election is schedule for December 4 2021 in Gambia. Therefore, this indicator is not applicable.
indicator: Elections taking place as scheduled pre-COVID

justification: There is no relevant information on the change in pattern in human trafficking in Gambia, relevant to COVID-19, causing an infogap. Although there is a news article that indicated the threat of the number of illegal immigrants crossing the border of Gambia and Senegal has increased. The government of Gambia struggles to protect the borders.

There were unrest in the county unrelated to COVID-19, therefore this indicator has an infogap. The unrest was caused by political means in Gambia. The present abuse of  people's human rights and claim dictatorships has caused the unrest. The unrest also occurred before the first COVID-19 case was reported in Gambia.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification: There is no significant information pertaining to civil unrest with relation to COVID-19. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: There is no relevant information on violence against health workers during the course of the pandemic in Gambia. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.

There is no information available for Gambia's primary school enrollment rate in 2020. According to the World Bank the latest available enrollment rate was 77% in 2018. Therefore, considering the outdated information, this indicator is considered an infogap. There is no available source date.

There is no information regarding a change in reported discrimination towards a specific group within the country of Gambia with relation to COVID-19. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification: There is no relevant information reported with regards to a change in internal displacement within Gambia but since the 23rd of March, the government has implemented movement restrictions across borders. It struggles to implement this due to the large informal sector. Considering the lack of information regarding change, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Internal Displacement and Mobility related to COVID-19

justification: There is no relevant information on the change of access to sexual and reproductive services in Gambia with regards to the pandemic. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap. Although, there is campaigning in Basse in the Upper River Region, to give women access and information on reproduction.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: There are no reports of change in domestic violence during the pandemic in Gambia, indicating an infogap. Although a news article did indicate that women are specifically at risk to domestic violence during the pandemic.

There are no relevant reports of changes in child or forced marriage in Gambia during the pandemic, indicating an infogap. Although a news article did indicate that due to closures of schools, girls are at risk of child marriage in Gambia during the pandemic.

There is no relevant information on authority of non-state armed groups that dictate and impose restrictions against COVID-19 during the pandemic in Gambia. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.

There are no reports of change in of a change in child labour due to the pandemic in Gambia, indicating an infogap. Although a news article did indicate that during this period, children are at risk to be exploited. The latest report of child labour in Gambia was in 2019 where the Gambian Government and US embassy were attempting to eliminate child exploitation.
There is no available information on a decreased/increased access for minorities to COVID-19 support in Gambia. Therefore, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: The latest information regarding the incarceration rate was in 2019. Therefore, the current incarceration rate is outdated. However, a news article reported that the Gambian president released 115 inmates to contain the spread of the COVID-19 virus, which indicates a decrease in the current incarceration rate.

There is no information pertaining to a change in the abuse of human rights relating to COVID-19, indicating an infogap. Although, news reports do state that the president of Gambia is abusing human rights through incorporating a dictatorship leaders style. However, this is unrelated to COVID-19.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: No current available data regarding the change of the poverty rate in Honduras during the COVID-19 emergency. According to the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) estimations, the poverty rate in Honduras could reach as high as 57.8%, while extreme poverty could increase from 18.7% to 20.5%. Therefore Honduras is among the countries that are expected to see the biggest increases in poverty in their population, due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This is mostly due to the previous economic situation of the country, which was characterized by very low growth, with structural gaps and an unsustainable development model, fragmented health systems and deep inequalities, according to the report. The economic consequences from the novel-coronavirus pandemic such as a steep decline in tourism and sharp drop in remittances are among the main causes of the increase of this indicator.
source: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC)

justification: According to CGTN, demonstrations related to COVID-19 in Ecuador have increased ((May 2020) since March 2020, as a consequence of the drastic economic measures implemented by the Government during the pandemic (wage cuts, reduction of staff in companies, extended lockdown and movement restrictions).
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: According to Central America Data, during February 2020, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) registered a 3.99% variation (since 02/2019). According to Central America Data the rise has been determined in part by the behavior of the prices of education services, hotels and restaurants. Changes in monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) were determined by the contribution of the item "Education" with 0.51 percentage points (pp), together with the items "Recreation and Culture" and "Hotels, Cafes and Restaurants" with 0.04 pp, each. On the contrary, "Transportation" contributed -0.18 pp to the monthly inflation. The increase of inflation in Honduras is therefore a consequence of Governmental measures.

According to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), COVID-19 restrictions and governments hardening borders, have forced non state armed groups to adapt to possible illegal drug market's disruptions, and to the increased competition for local markets.
On the one hand, ACLED reported that violence targeting civilians has decreased significantly in all three countries of the Northern Triangle (Honduras-El Salvador-Guatemala) since the official start of the pandemic. Also, in March 2020, extortion decreased by almost 80% compared to the same period of 2019.
On the other hand, inter-gang fighting has increased across the country. The overall change of the indicator is therefore logged as "increased" since the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic (March-May 2020) due to the Governmental measures implemented in order to contain the spread of the novel-coronavirus.
source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED)

justification: According to InSight Crime, the events of human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies have increased since the beginning of the pandemic (March-May 2020). Cases of gun abuse and torture by authorities to enforce the confinement measures have been reported in the country. The driver of the change of this indicator is reported as behavioral, as these events of violence, even if dependent on armed forces, are not attributable to governmental measures.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification:
According to the ACAPS report, the humanitarian access in Honduras remained stable since the beginning of the pandemic (March-June 2020), for this reason the indicator has been logged as "no change". The overall access ranking attributed to the country is 2, mostly due to the ongoing hostilities, restriction of access to services and assistance and restrictions of movements following governmental measures. 
It is therefore to notice that hostility in the country has increased since the beginning of the confinement measures, as several events of extortion and intimidation crimes from street gangs have been reported. The presence of structured gangs and transnational criminal organizations brings have increased crime risks across the country.
Garda World also highlights other constraints in accessing the country, such as severe risks of natural disasters, especially in the rainy season, such as  floods, landslides, and storms. 
Routine vaccination for all travelers is foreseen and includes vaccinations for diphtheria, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, influenza, measles, mumps, pertussis, rubella, varicella, etc.
Finally another possible constraint to humanitarian access is the increase of politically motivated demonstrations, since President Juan Orlando Hernandez took office in January 2018.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) reported that cases of discrimination and stigma towards medical, nursing and emergency personnel in Honduras have increased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-July  2020). The driver of this behaviors is the fear of contagion, and the consideration that healthcare workers have higher probabilities of contracting the novel-coronavirus. No cases of physical violence against health workers have been reported in the country. Despite this factor, the change of the indicator has been logged as "increased" since of the beginning of the pandemic as discrimination is a form of psychological violence.
source: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)

justification: According to United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), formal employment has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 crisis (March- May 2020); restrictions on mobilization by the state of emergency both at borders and in cities has a direct negative impact on the generation of income and livelihood opportunities for an important segment of the population. The Independent Federation of Workers of Honduras (FITH) indicated that more than 200,000 employees have been suspended and fired due to the COVID emergency.
source: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) retrieved through ReliefWeb

justification: According to Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), hospitals and health centers all over the country have reported a lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) and resources to care for patients. The availability of non-COVID-19 related medical supply has decreased since the beginning of the pandemic (March-September 2020) as a result of the unpreparedness of the country's health system for an emergency, and as a consequence of the corruption surrounding mobile hospitals, as reported by various national and international media sources.  Another factor is the lack of medical personnel; according to the Medical College of Honduras, more than 40% of healthcare workers contracted the virus.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies
source: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) retrieved through ReliefWeb

justification: According to a local academic institution, after universities closure following the preventive measured implemented by the Government during the COVID-19 pandemic, authorities in Honduras launched their own online platforms, providing distance-learning contents to students, open resources and applications, in order to ensure continuity in higher education programmes (March-June 2020). Governmental measures have therefore determined the increase of this indicator since the beginning of the novel-coronavirus pandemic.
source: Universidad Abierta de Recoleta (UAR) retrieved through Reliefweb

justification: In Honduras, the National Committee to Prevent Torture and Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment (MNP-CONAPREV), has presented a petition to the Supreme Court of Justice to protect at-risk prisoners from exposure to COVID-19. The aim of this initiative is the early release those who are particularly vulnerable. This category includes detainees suffering from chronic diseases (such as diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular illnesses), those over the age of 60 and people living with HIV/AIDS. The request was filed in March 2020 and accepted by the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court on April 1, 2020.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), population's access to humanitarian services or assistance has decreased during the COVID-19 emergency compared to the beginning of 2020 (March-May 2020). According to the source, 794,000 people are currently affected by limited access to humanitarian assistance, due to the low response capacity of the integrated medical care networks (insufficient medical personnel), low percentage of drugs and supplies in health care facilities, and poor availability of tools and medical equipment, and most of all the unequal distribution in primary care, which precludes part of the population in need to access humanitarian assistance. Therefore, Governmental measures are driving the change of this indicator.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance
source: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) retrieved through ReliefWeb

justification: According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), access to primary and secondary school was limited as a consequence of the suspension of face-to-face classes during the COVID-19 emergency (March-May 2020). This governmental measure was implemented in order to prevent and control the spread of the pandemic in the country.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools
source: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) retrieved through ReliefWeb

justification:
The number of Egyptians with mental disorders increased during the pandemic. The most frequent illnesses are depression, anxiety disorders, substance uses disorder (SUD), and OCD. Men are more impacted by depression and SUD, while women represented more cases of OCD and anxiety disorders.
Egypt’s Health Ministry set up two hotlines to provide psychological support.
source: Journal of Psychiatry and Psychiatric Disorders

justification:
On the one hand, with the reduction of income and formal employment, many underemployed and unemployed people seek to guarantee their means of living by participating in informal jobs. On the other hand, people in informal jobs have also seen a reduction in employment. 
Reports also point out that the pandemic has revealed the informality and precariousness of certain sectors, like that of tourism which is one of the pillars of Costa Rican economy and one of the most affected by the pandemic.

In March when the state of alarm was declared, series of government measures were put in place regarding labour laws. Most notorious were the reduction of working hours up to 50% for employers who could justify the impacts of the pandemic; 'suspension' of contracts instead of dismissals; teleworking was also regulated. These authorisations are considered temporal for the time of emergency. Pregnant and breastfeeding women are protected from these measures.
In July, it was also approved that, from 2020 to 2024, public holidays will be moved to Mondays in order to create 'long weekends' and boost national tourism.
Protests against economic measures and asking for more protection for the unemployed and underemployed were also held in July.
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

justification:
Personal remittances have affected Central America, including Costa Rica. This latter, nevertheless, does not depend so much on personal remittances (0.9% of the GDP in 2019, low compared to other Central American countries). Estimations put a figure of about -13% in the variation of personal remittances. 

On the other hand, Nicaragua does depend on remittances from Costa Rica, which have been highly affected by the pandemic.

Since April, Costa Rica has seen a decrease in its monthly inflation, reaching its lowest point in July (-0.17), finally showing a positive trend in September (0.3).
Analysts have related this negative tendency to the containment measures and its impacts: unemployment, a decrease in consumption, generalised low inflation for important commercial partners, low petrol prices, etc.
The recent relatively positive trend could be due to the progressive openness of the country to receive international tourists.

In the last years, Costa Rica had seen its poverty rate decreasing, but this trend has been disrupted by the pandemic. Containment measures have hardly hit the country which is highly dependent on international tourism and, despite its relatively strong health system, has had increasing COVID-19 cases since July. Estimations in May projected an increase of 9 percentual points in the poverty rate, which last year remained at about 21%. To fight poverty and unemployment, the government is now negotiating with the IMF, which has been widely protested against across the country.

No information is found for household disposable income in 2020. It registered a positive trend until 2016 (last data available in the OECD iLibrary). It is now expected to be negatively impacted by the pandemic, as unemployment continues to grow and the health system is also close to collapse.
source: INEC (National Institute of Statistics and Census)

justification: 216700 tertiary students were affected by the closing of education services (UNESCO). Most universities are now running their classes online, with an important presence of Microsoft Teams as the main tool. The differential impact of the pandemic and online education according to socio-economic status is also made evident, as some students may lack the resources to continue studying or do so online, without proper internet access.Another factor that has been underlined is the high proportion of students enrolled in private institutions and what can be the consequences of the pandemic. These institutions, as they depend on private funding, could face serious challenges to keep offering their services, leaving many students in debts, and displaced from higher education (Forbes).
source: UNESCO; IESALC (Instituto Internacional para la Educación Superior en América Latina y el Caribe)

justification: According to UNESCO 960438 primary and secondary students were affected by the closure of schools since March. The government has announced that the rest of the academic year will be online (until the 23rd of December). Since March a series of programmes have been developed to support online learning, reaching about 55% of students according to the Ministry of Public Education. For students with no internet conection, programmes like "Hogares Conectados" (Connected Homes) have been developed, which aim to provide computers and/or internet to the beneficiaries. Certain communities are especially affected by non-internet connection, for whom TV and radio support have been developed with the programme "Aprende en casa" (Learn at Home) to support online education at several school levels. The Ministry of Public Education has done this by public-private partnerships (PPP).
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools
source: Ministry of Public Education (Ministerio Educación Pública, MEP)

justification: Since March a series of programmes have been developed to support online learning, reaching about 55% of students according to the Ministry of Public Education. For students with no internet conection, programmes like "Hogares Conectados" (Connected Homes) have been developed, which aim to provide computers and/or internet to the beneficiaries. Certain communities are especially affected by non-internet connection, for whom TV and radio support have been developed with the programme "Aprende en casa" (Learn at Home) to support online education at several school levels. The Ministry of Public Education has done this by public-private partnerships (PPP), for instance with Microsoft to implement Microsoft Meats as a main tool.
source: Ministry of Public Education (Ministerio Educación Pública, MEP)

justification:
Not much information is found on the effects of COVID-19 pandemic on child, early or forced marriage. In January 2017 a law that forbids marriage for people below 18 years old was passed, which was supported by UNICEF and other institutions. The implementation of this law has been read as especially challenging among Indigenous and Afro-descendent communities.
Child and teenage marriage is related to early pregnancy, which has considerably declined since 2000, but is still considered a problem in Costa Rica (UNFPA).

According to the UNFPA, the fight against early marriages and pregnancy becomes ever-more urgent during the pandemic, due to the greater vulnerability status of girls.

This is considered an infogap. Data indicates that low-income households in developing and emerging countries will face a significant dip in their household disposable income however data specifically based on Afghanistan is unavailable.

There is an Infogap for this indicator as no recent data is currently available. However predictions for the future believe that Remittances are set for a sharp decline, as unemployment rise and many Afghan workers return from host countries remittances inflows could fall by as much as 50% by the end of the year.

A national primary school enrolment rate is unavailable, some schools have not reopened and others have progressively opened across the country therefore there isn't a national primary school enrolment rate. This is considered an infogap.

Personal remittances received in Nigeria have decreased, as the major economies which Nigeria rely on for remittances have deteriorated under lockdown measures. These major economies include countries such as Britain, France, Italy, Spain, and the US which account for about 54 percent of remittance incomes in Nigeria. Remittances from these countries have already declined dramatically; for example, some payment companies in Europe are seeing declines of 80 to 90 percent in remittance payments to Africa. It has also been stated that remittances in a country, like Nigeria, plays an important role in the contribution to the country's GDP.
source: IFPRI International Food Policy Research Institute

justification: Due to government measures implemented in Nigeria to try and curb the spread of the virus, such as border closures, lockdown measures, and movement restrictions have had an impact on the economy. Border closures have pushed prices higher. According to Nairametrics and Trading economics Nigerias inflation rate rose to 13.22% in August 2020 which was the highest recorded in 29 months. Due to the COVID-19 measures, prices of commodities have also been affected, which includes air transport and medical services.

No information can be found related to the availability of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies in FSM. Only information related to priority medical supplies can be found.  This is logged as an infogap.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: No recent immunisation campaigns can be found.  this is logged as an infogap.
No specific information can be found regarding mental health changes in Micronesia.  this is logged as an infogap.
This is logged as an infogap. No changes in alcohol consumption or substance abuse can be found for FSM.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: Not many sources pertain to immunisation campaigns in Israel (unrelated to a COVID-19 vaccine). The most relevant source states that the demand for a new flu vaccine in Israel might be higher this year. “In previous years, we had a coverage rate that allowed for vaccination for anyone who wanted it...This year, if the demand is higher than the supply, we won’t have enough flu shots for everyone.” The reasons why there might be a shortage is attributed to higher demand (which is assumingly because of fear of COVID-19). However, as there is not a shortage yet and definite reasons for a shortage is not attributed to COVID-19, this indicator remains as an infogap.

There is a decreased access to elective surgery and non-essential procedures for patients in Israel in September 2020. The Health Ministry Director General Chezy Levy stated that “We expect to end the next 10 days with an increase of 200-300 serious, ventilated or critical patients...I ask you to treat this situation as an emergency situation for the healthcare system. Hospitals must end elective, non-essential procedures.” The reasoning behind this is so that hospitals can dedicate all of their resources to the pandemic response according to the source linked.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: Sources only mention the lack of COVID-19 equipment (PPE) in Israel, yet no article provides any information about the change in availability of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: No sources specifically provide information on how COVID-19 affected the voter turnout in Israel. This is possibly because the election was held in March of 2020, which is before a large number of cases were seen in Israel. The first source linked states that "Due to coronavirus fears, voter turnout in next week's election is expected to be much lower..." However, as shown in the alternative source, the voter turnout was actually the highest it has ever been since 1999. Therefore, one can infer that COVID-19 did not negatively impact the voter turnout, but since no source specifically states so, this indicator was flagged as an infogap.
indicator: Voter turnout in latest national elections that took place since beginning of covid pandemic

justification: Most sources provide information about violence against health workers prior to 2020 and the pandemic. Most incidents are related to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Palestine in Gaza. However, no articles relevant to COVID-19 as an influence to violence against health workers in Israel was found. No source date is added to the source obtained.

In the month of May, the number of complaints about domestic violence in Israel has risen by 112% compared to April (reported by the Welfare and Social Services Ministry in Israel). As a spike in domestic violence complaints surfaced, thousands of people have gathered at a rally, as a result, in Tel Aviv on Monday calling for government action to end violence against women. Protesters gathered hoping to gain government action for the $(US)71 million approved in 2017 for national programs to prevent domestic violence which has not yet been transferred to relevant authorities. The reason for the rise in domestic violence cases have been attributed to the lockdown measures imposed by the government due to COVID-19. The article states that: "Police and social service organizations have reported a major rise in domestic violence complaints since the start of the coronavirus crisis, which has been blamed for exacerbating tensions as people were confined together by lockdown measures.

No source states that Israel has exhibited a change in the number of prisoners across the country due to COVID-19. The only relevant source (linked) insinuates that there was an increase in arrests made due to COVID-19 regulations that were breached. Israeli police have arrested over 300 people at a gathering at a religious shrine as it violates COVID-19 regulations. Whether a change in the number of prisoners was seen across the country is undetermined as the sources do not state so.
No relevant sources were found concerning a change in child labour in Israel, relevant to COVID-19.
No sources have reported a change in authority of non-state armed groups relevant to COVID-19 in Israel.

No sources pertain to a change in child, early and forced marriages in Israel, in relation to COVID-19. The source linked states that there is no publicly available government data on child marriage in Israel. It therefore makes it difficult finding information pertaining to this indicator. It should be noted that Israel has committed to eliminating child, early and forced marriage by 2030 in line with target 5.3 of the Sustainable Development Goals. Child marriage is illegal in Israel. Whether it is increasing/decreasing and whether COVID-19 has an influence is unknown due to the lack of sources. Note that the source linked has no source date.

No reports state that a change in human trafficking or migrant smuggling has occurred as a result of COVID-19 in Israel. In fact, when viewing the source, Israel fully meets the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking and is therefore at a 'tier 1'. The alternative source states that Israel is one of the top countries in the world combating human trafficking for the ninth consecutive year. One can therefore infer that incidents of human trafficking and migrant smuggling may be low which is why no sources indicate a rise or decrease in human trafficking due to COVID-19. No source date is provided.

Hundreds of Israelis have gathered at Tel Aviv to protest against a second nationwide lockdown which was imposed due to a rise in COVID-19 cases. Many protests have been reported throughout Israel in recent months over the government's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. In the alternative source it is seen that the Israeli government has actually banned protests due to COVID-19 regulations. Essentially this was not effective as these regulations have sparked protests across the country.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: Many of the protests that have increased throughout this year is in relation to Israelis demanding the resignation of the Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. In October 2020 tens of thousands of Israelis have gathered stating that the prime minister is unfit to rule while on trial for his corruption charges. COVID-19 also has an influence as the protesters have accused him of mismanaging the response to the coronavirus pandemic. The current lockdown regulations allow people to gather only within one kilometer of their homes.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification: No sources found in relation to the indicator have stated that access to sexual and reproductive services have declined during lockdown in Israel. The source that is linked states that COVID-19 positive pregnant mothers in Israel have to deliver alone with the midwife and are hospitalized alone. No source states that midwives are not able to work or that there is a decline in access to these types of services. It is certain that giving birth during a pandemic comes with extra difficulties due to precautionary measures in Israel.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: No reliable and relevant source pertains to internally displaced individuals within Israel with relation to COVID-19.
indicator: Internal Displacement and Mobility related to COVID-19

justification: There is a lack of sources relating to violence and discrimination against minorities in Israel. This indicator was left as an infogap.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification: No information is available with regards to a lack of access for minorities to COVID-19 medical support in Israel. Most sources relate to Israel and the Gaza strip where Palestinians are seen as minorities that lack access to COVID-19 supplies under Israeli control. However, considering that Palestinians are not minorities in Israel itself, this indicator is considered an infogap.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: According to human right accusations made, it is stated that Muslims are targeted and scapegoated for spreading COVID-19 in countries like Israel. The source states that the Israeli government and prime minister is laying the groundwork for placing the blame on Palestinians (Muslim Palestinian Israeli citizens) for spreading COVID-19. The Prime Minister singled this minority out by stating that "unfortunately instructions are not strictly adhered to in the Arab sector" and asked for their cooperation. According to the author, this was the Prime Minister's subtle way of pinning the potential catastrophe (of COVID-19) on Palestinian Israeli citizens.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification: The abuse of human rights by Israeli authorities have risen since the outbreak of COVID-19 within prisons. Reports have emerged that Israeli authorities have been using COVID-19 as a tool of suppression and intimidation against Palestinians prisoners inside Israeli prisons. For example, Israeli interrogators have even threatened to expose Palestinian prisoners to the virus. There is also a medical negligence towards Palestinian prisoners where authorities are  failing to supply the facilities sanitisers and masks. Palestinian prisoners have been deprived of family visits and communications, including child detainees, as well as restrictions on money transfers to purchase in-prison goods. The UN pointed out that Israel had released hundreds of Israeli prisoners, but failed to do the same for their Palestinian counterparts, which indicates discriminatory treatment, in violation of international law. These human rights violations have persisted since the outbreak of COVID-19 especially for Palestinians in prison in Israel.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification: No sources specifically pertain to the monthly inflation rate of Israel and what effect COVID-19 has had. The most relevant sources linked have provided data on the annual inflation rate which is expected to decrease by -1.9% in 2020 and increase to 0.5% in 2021. The alternative source states that "the shekel has depreciated, which can help Israel’s export and inflation rate recover later." This source insinuates that COVID-19 has negatively impacted the inflation rate. The source further states that "The impact of the virus on Israel’s economy will eventually come down to the outbreak’s severity and duration." No source date is provided for the first source.

No sources are present concerning COVID-19's effect on Israel's poverty rate. The most relevant source states that two-million Israeli's have lost their income due to COVID-19. Therefore great fear is present for middle-class families who might be in poverty in 2021. This source is the closest source indicating that the poverty rate might increase. However, since it does not specifically state so, this indicator is labelled as an infogap.
No sources are present relating to a change in personal remittances for Israel.

The most relevant source available states that the average household net-adjusted disposable income per capita is USD 33 604 a year in Israel. However, no date is attached to this figure and it is therefore uncertain whether this relates to 2020. Furthermore, this is a 'net' statistic. No relevant household disposable income statistic could be found. The source also gives no indication of the effect of COVID-19. No source date was available for the link attached.

Relevant sources stating that staple food prices have changed because of COVID-19 could not be found. However, one source stated that business owners have taken matters into their own hands by raising the cost of basic food prices by using COVID-19 as an excuse. One can therefore infer that food prices have increased (informally) even though the government has fixed food prices. Following complaints from citizens over raising food prices, the Economy Ministry has begun intensively enforcing regulations in food stores across the country to prevent businesses from raising prices at their own terms.
Sources concerning a change in school feeding programmes for Israel are not available.
No sources relating to a change in Israel's net primary school enrollment rate are found.

The ability for vendors to sell their products has decreased as government orders are to shut down Israel’s open-air food markets due to COVID-19 regulations. However, supermarkets are allowed to remain open. Therefore, access to essential goods have not decreased for civilians, but vendor's ability to make a living have decreased for those who work and sell their products at open-air markets.

Access to higher education facilities have decreased in Israel in the sense that online learning has replaced in-person contact classes. Universities in Israel are expected to continue online learning even after COVID-19 cases have subsided. For example, Tel Aviv University is expected to extend and continue offering its virtual courses by implementing online learning into the regular curriculum and the application process. Therefore, COVID-19 has essentially changed the structure and programmes of higher education in Israel, as online learning is continued to be used.

Israel is experiencing a decreasing food security for its population and is expected to see an increase in the number of food insecure people. The article states that the BDO consultant company and Leket Israel organization reports that roughly 145,000 additional people in Israel are predicted to enter into the cycle of food insecurity by the end of 2020. The total number of food insecure people will rise to two million people in Israel. The COVID-19 crisis has increased the demand for food aid. justification: It is undetermined whether the price of hand sanitizers have increased in Israel. This is because at first, consumers were complaining that stores are taking advantage of the COVID-19 scare to hike the price of popular hand sanitizer products. Super-Pharm, the country’s largest pharmacy chain, stated that the increasing prices that the consumers were complaining of is because of human error and not policy. As a result, Israel’s Ministry of Economy and Industry announced that the country’s major pharmacy and supermarket chains, including Super-Pharm, Shufersal Ltd., and Rami Levy Hashikma Marketing 2006 Ltd., have agreed to limit the price of alcohol-based hand sanitizer to NIS 9.9 (approximately $2.7) per 100 milliliters. Israel’s Ministry of Economy therefore ordered prices of hand sanitizers to be capped at a set price. The prices should therefore remain unchanged. The fear of COVID-19, and the associated behavioral changes, has increased the demand for these type of products. However, as prices are capped, it remains unchanged and can not further increase even with the growing demand.
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification:
Increased xenophobic discourse is reported since the pandemic started. A study of COES Comunicación reveals that conversations that involve xenophobia and discrimination have increased in a 62% since the first case of COVID-19 in Costa Rica (March to June), and that the figure rises with the increase of the cases. The main target of the offenses are Nicaraguan people, followed by Asians. 5% of the messages refer to Costa Ricans living in places with high risks of contagion. The majority of these messages blame these people of transmitting and increasing COVID-19 cases, and also assure they will be the ones collapsing the health system.

Positive messages are also triggered in this sense with the approval of same-sex marriage in the country and Black Lives Matter movement.

Other cases of discrimination involve some politicians, especially those close to the Northern border, making xenophobic remarks against Nicaraguans. Media (CRHoy) also reports in the Northern region locals pressured to chase out Nicaraguans from a hostal that was offered to them to quarantine. Similarly, a violent attack to a hostal that was attending COVID-19 positive Indigenous people also reflects the racism and xenophobia boosted by the pandemic.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification:
Not much data is found on the pandemic's effects on human trafficking and migrant smuggling. Nevertheless, as exposed by the UN, the situation is expected to worsen with the economic and sanitary crisis, as ever-more people find themselves in desperate conditions and are vulnerable to trafficking and exploitation. In Costa Rica, this especially applies to  migrants from Nicaragua, in a context of border closures. Moreover, the working and living conditions of these people make them especially susceptible to the virus.

By the same token, human trafficking for sexual exploitation is also expected to increase and adopt new forms under the pandemic (e.g. creating online material).
source: REDTRAM (Red Iberoamericana de Fiscales Especializados contra la Trata de Personas y Tráfico de Migrantes)

justification:
A CIEP (research) study reveals that at the beginning of the pandemic Alvarado's government gained popularity and confidence to deal with COVID-19. This was coherent with the positive results of Costa Rica during the first months (with a low mortality rate), but with the second wave and worse prospects the government again lost confidence and popularity, with 50% of survey respondents reporting a negative opinion on the pandemic's management. While in April the main concern for the population was coronavirus, unemployment is now the most popular fear among Costa Ricans. In August, a series of demonstrations were organised against the president Carlos Alvarado and the restrictive measures.

In July, the president announced negotiations were being done with the IMF to get to an agreement and manage the economic crisis caused by the pandemic. In September the government presented the proposal: a credit of US$1750million for a three year period to stabilise the economy. Overcrowding is particularly worrying in the COVID-19 context, as social distance is especially challenging.

justification:
Since the beginning of the pandemic the government has made declarations pointing out Nicaraguan government mismanagement and the danger of Nicaraguan migrants to spread the virus, while reinforcing border controls. In May, government representatives asked the Panamerican Health Organization (OPS) to evaluate Nicaraguan situation regarding COVID-19. This reinforces the stigmatization of Nicaraguan migrants, which is also reflected in other openly xenophobic practices and discourses.
In Los Chiles health area (close to the Nicaraguan border) it was ordered that no undocumented person would be attended and that authorities would be called, a guideline that was later put off due to its discriminatory nature. Alfredo Córdoba, the major of San Carlos (Northern region) also made openly xenophobic declarations, stating that Nicaraguans did not have the culture to quarantine, and that Costa Ricans were very "educated" but Nicaraguans would not listen to the indications.Laura Bonilla, the president of the exporters' group (CADEXCO) also stated that "the great problem (regarding the pandemic) was the migration of sick people".
