According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), at the end of 2019, there were 102,000 Nicaraguans migrants, 86,994 of whom was seeking asylum in the Latin America and Caribbean Region. The migratory flow in Nicaragua is mainly directed towards the outside of the country, as the number of Nicaraguans forced to leave increases due to political persecution. In the state of emergency from COVID-19, a reverse migration flow has been reported, as a consequence of the restrictions imposed by the authorities due to the COVID-19 emergency; the majority of migrants in asylum countries were unable to generate income, thus becoming more dependent on humanitarian assistance. During the state of emergency, Nicaraguan nationals have also experienced problems with obtaining identification documents. UNHCR also reported the COVID-19 impact on mental health as a further cause that pushes migrants to return to Nicaragua (accordingly, the drivers of the change of the indicator are both behavioral and governmental). In this context, various countries in Central America have opened humanitarian corridors for stranded Nicaraguans wanting to return to their country. As reported by several sources, Nicaraguan returnees faced hunger and fear of the novel-coronavirus contagion in the long-term wait to carry out the COVID-19 test at the country border. As of September 2020, more than 58,000 Nicaraguan migrants have returned, mainly due to the economic impact of the pandemic. The indicator has thus increased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency.
indicator: Return of migrant workers  from abroad
source: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) retrieved through Reliefweb

When mobility restrictions are lifted and borders open once again, we are every likely to see a surge in Nicaraguans fleeing the country, according to UNHCR report. Therefore, the cause of the decrease of this indicator is governmental measures.

source: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) retrieved through Reliefweb

Not much information is found about IO or INGOs suspending activities in Costa Rica due to novel-coronavirus outbreak. In this context, new projects have emerged to deal with the challenges driven by the pandemic. For instance, Costa Rican government and the WHO have joined to launch a COVID-19 technology pool of free access.

Moreover, according to UN OCHA, international funding increased in Costa Rica compared to last year. These funds were especially focused on migrants and assylum seekers, as Costa Rica receives many people in these conditions.

Containment measures of the pandemic have, nevertheless, affected the services some of these IOs offer, both in its focus (for instance now centring in taking food to at risk populations) and its means (the UNHCR reported closing physical offices and now works remotely). This latter can result in less effective operations. Moreover, the UNHCR also reported severe underfunding for its projects in 2020.

justification:
Containment measures in Costa Rica, which were especially strict during the first months of the outbreak (closure of borders, mobility restrictions, etc.), as well as the economic downturn not only in Costa Rica, but at a global scale, have severely affected local and national NGOs. These NGOs, dedicated to a wide range of issues (environmental conservation, food banks, homeless attendance, etc.), depend on funds and volunteers, crucially international ones, which have been critically impacted by the pandemic. This has led to the stagnation of many projects in several sectors.

On the other hand, the COVID-19 outbreak has also boosted other projects directly or indirectly related to the disease and its impacts. For instance, many groups have organised to help most vulnerable populations with food and medical attendance. NGOs have also called attention to the government when discrimination has been perceived, for instance, in medical guidelines. These are especially focalised in the border with Nicaragua, where a humanitarian crisis has been formed due to health requisites to enter the country. In this context, NGOs have proven crucial.

According to ACAPS in July 2020, overall humanitarian access has deteriorated in Costa Rica since the pandemic. Overall, the country was given a scale 1 out of 5 with a score of 2 regarding restriction of access to services and assistance.

In rapid needs assessments of the UNHCR, the impact of COVID-19 on Nicaraguan and Venezuelan population in Costa Rica were studied from July to August 2020. It was reported that only 35% of Nicaraguan households had received some form of assitance since the preventive isolation measures started. Of these, 52% received assitance from NGOs and/or UN agencies and 43% from the government (mainly in food items). Half of this assistance was 'in-kind'.
For Venezuelan households, 64% of the surveyed reported receiving some form of assistance since COVID-19 outbreak,  of which 53% were assisted by NGOs and/or UN agencies and 34% by the government (mainly in food items). Just over half of the assistance was 'in-kind'.

Nevertheless, there is no straighforward information stating the relationship between the COVID-19 pandemic and the access to humanitarian services or assistance, which is why this indicator is marked with an InfoGap. It could be reasoned that the economic impacts and containment measures to face the pandemic have affected the funding, prospects and the way in which organisations work. The UNHCR for instance reported closing physical offices and now offering certain services remotely, online or by phone. This can further impact the ability of people to access information and aid.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification:
No active armed groups hold authority in the country for 2020.

Last year in July, an allegedly armed group published a video calling for a violent coup. They defined as far-right and were called "Frente Patriota 7 de Julio". The authors of the video were localised and prosecuted.

Other violent encounters have involved Indigenous leaders, two of whom were killed in March  2019 and February 2020.

Access to water and sanitary services in Costa Rica is especially challenging for certain populations, like those in informal settlements and for migrant and asylum seekers. With the pandemic the accessibility to personal hygiene and sanitation items has remained a crucial concern. According to the SIWI (Stockholm International Water Institute) for the period from March to May 2020, the government established a series of measures focused on the more extensive provision of water and 'hand washing' spots in priority locations (schools, health establishments, public stations, markets, etc.). Among other things, the government has assured water to households who could not afford the payment of the service, including in informal settlements.

Nevertheless, the UNHCR reports that between July and August 2020 a percentage of Nicaraguan and Venezuelan asylum seekers and refugees faced difficulties to access personal hygiene and sanitation. A 10% of the Nicaraguan households surveyed did not have access to potable water whenever they needed it. And almost 5% of household reported household members did not wash their hands regularly with both water and soap, and only over 27% regularly use hand sanitiser. Among Venezuelan housholds, 6% did not report having access to potable water whenever they needed it, and only 1% reported household members did not wash their hands regularly with both soap and water. And just over 25% regularly use hand sanitiser.
indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification:
No data for general mortality rate in 2020. It is expected to grow due to COVID-19 pandemic. While at the beginning mortality rate was the lowest in the continent (at 0.81% in May), cases and mortality rate are now growing, and there is a worry about a potential collapse of the health system. 

Coronavirus mortality rate in October was at 1.23%.

There is no clear evidence of reported impacts of the pandemic on the access to sexual and reproductive services.

The OHCHR estimates unwanted pregnancies and sexual and reproductive health in general will be negatively impacted by the pandemic in the context of Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). The UNFPA estimates that the use of and access to contraceptives will have decreased with the pandemic. Mainly due to a) disruptions and delays in supply chains, b) health systems' alterations that now focus on mitigating and treating COVID-19 (deviating resources and staff to this cause), and c) decrease of demand of sexual and reproductive health due to the fear to attend health centres and contract the virus or due to mobility restrictions. Moreover, other factors can also influence this access, for example households' income reduction
and the focus of women on basic needs other than their own health. The report, published in August 2020, estimates these impacts will be relatively low in Costa Rica compared to the LAC context.

In June 2020 the INAMU (Women's National Institute), the UNFPA, the CCSS (Costa Rican health system) and the Ministry of Health launched a campaign to promote reproductive and sexual health during the pandemic. This campaign mainly focuses on pregnancy, lactation, shared responsibility in housework and the prevention of gender-based violence. It aims, for instance, to encourage pregnant women to attend regular health controls despite the message to "stay home". It also encourages breastfeeding, and actions for mothers to prevent or to deal with COVID-19. 

Appart from this the government has also taken other actions to protect pregnant mothers, for instance by particularly protecting their labour rights amid the pandemic. In May 2020, Costa Rica also signed the "Joint statement on Protecting Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights and Promoting Gender-responsiveness in the COVID-19 crisis".

Nevertheless, in May, feminist and other groups reported the CCSS left many of these services unattended during the pandemic, and asked for a better access to contraceptives.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification:
Since the novel-coronavirus outbreak, the government has taken a series of measures to extend water access and infrastructure around the country.

In March, AyA (the sewage system) recognised the infrastructure deficit of water especially in certain points of the country (some rural areas, informal settlements, etc.). Some incidents in the region of Guanacaste, made the AyA to prevent people from drinking tap water (related to contamination with arsenic), and led the government to provide tank trucks in the area. In April, calls for a responsible use of water were made from the government and main water and sewage operators (AyA, ASADAS, ESPH, etc.).

The government recognised the emergency of water shortages amid the pandemic and took a series of measures. According to the SIWI (Stockholm International Water Institute) for the period from March to May 2020, the Costa Rican government established a series of measures focused on the more extensive provision of water and 'hand washing' spots in priority locations (schools, health establishments, public stations, markets, etc.). Among other things, the government has assured water to households who could not afford the payment of the service, including in informal settlements.

In June, access to potable water was declared a human right in Costa Rica. In July, a project to extend water infrastructure in the region of Guanacaste was also formalised. Better access to potable water was considered a benefit for the economy of the region (in terms of agriculture and tourism), as well as to combat COVID-19.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification:
No great structural changes in public services funding are reported, despite since the COVID-19 outbreak the focus on health services and mitigation measures is noted. Moreover, plans and projections to restructure public funding in the short run are being debated.

Costa Rica is noted to have a relatively strong funding for public health and education, which helped the country to be praised as an example of success by UN agencies during the first months of the pandemic, until May/June. The government (CGR) also reports an increase in the public funding to the CCSS (Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social; national social security).

Credits and donations that were formerly arranged for other ends were also restructured to mitigate the pandemic and its impacts. For instance, credits negotiated with the Inter-American Development Bank and the French Agency for Development (for a total of US$380 million) for the decarbonisation of the Costa Rican economy were later, in May, agreed to be used for the CCSS.

In July 2020, the OECD report of Costa Rica encouraged this expenditure in public health as well as in cash transfers to mitigate the economic and social impacts of the pandemic. The OECD report and the CGR (Costa Rican tax office) highlight certain inefficiencies of public services funding and call for a better management.

By October 2020, the president of the country, Carlos Alvarado, is calling for budget and financial adjustments for a reduction of the national debt. In September, the negotiations with the IMF, which involved tax increases and the sale of statal actives, were widely rejected by the opposition and civil society groups, provoking protests of up to 16 days.
source: Contraloría General de la República (CGR; Costa Rican inspection organism of public funding)

justification:
There is no data for primary school enrolment rate in 2020. For 2019, this figure was 99.3%, one of the highest in Latin America. 

Since March, schools have been closed as a response to the pandemic, and education will remain online at least until December 2020. Although the government has established a series of programmes to support education remotely (via TV, radio, internet), connectivity and access to devices have remained a challenge and affects particularly to rural and low socio-economic areas. This can have an effect on enrolment rate for certain sectors.

Moreover, the BBC reports the low birth rate trend is affecting the education structure, leaving many remote areas with less students, less resources and, hence, potentially affecting the enrolment rate in these areas.

The UNHCR (in "rapid needs assesment: impact of COVID-19 on the Venezuelan population in Costa Rica") reported by August 2020 that 8% of the households with school-aged children do not have acccess to the internet, and 12% do not have acess to educational materials or activities.

There is no solid data on Costa Ricans working abroad looking forward to return to their country. It is reported that the majority of Costa Ricans working abroad live in the USA, and that the pandemic has found this population particularly vulnerable, as, in June, the rate of deaths was higher for Costa Ricans than the US average.

There is scattered data on Costa Ricans travelling or temporarily working abroad that were not able to return at the beginning of the pandemic due to the mobility restrictions and cancelled flights. Repatriation flights were organised for these people in the first months of the pandemic.
indicator: Return of migrant workers  from abroad

justification:
No national elections were held in 2020. Latest national elections were in 2018, and the next will be held in 2022.
In February 2020 (before the pandemic outbreak in Costa Rica), municipal elections were held with a high levels of abstention (58.6%), that has decreased in last years.
indicator: Voter turnout in latest national elections that took place since beginning of covid pandemic

justification:
There is no monitored evolution of prices of personal hybiene and sanitation items. Since COVID-19 outbreak in March, the guidelines developed by the government encouraged the use of these products and their demand and production multiplied by over 4 times according to some media reports (Semanario Universidad).

In March, facing the huge escalation in the demand of sanitary products and the potential increase of prices and abusive practices of the market, the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Trade (MEIC) confirmed it would regulate the prices of disinfectant and cleaning items to assure a wide access. The Ministry briefly studied the consumer prices of these products around in supermarkets and other establishments. According to media reports, based on the Ministry's data collection, disparities of gel prices ranged up to a 44% in different sale points. The 25th of March it was resolved that prices would not be regulated. 
In April, a member of the parliament raised another proposal to exempt sanitary and cleaning items from the VAT, which is now 13%. These measures did not take place, but the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Trade (MEIC) stated that prices were being studied and that abusive prices would not be tolerated.
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Vaccination services were disrupted due to the covid related lockdown from April 15. Services were resumed on May 3.

indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: According to UNDP data, 90% of food is imported  in Maldives and the imports increased in January 2020 and February 2020.  In order to respond to COVID-19 shortages the government has identified 17 crops which they will produce. Moreover, the government is leasing out empty land for 3 years to farmers which they could sell on an online portal (that has also be developed by the government).  The report further states that government put a maximum retail price on food as there was a chance retailers could have sold it at higher prices due to COVID-19.

In a press briefing in March 2020 President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih  mentioned that there are no shortages of food for the next ten months. Info gap as no clear reports of either positive or negative impact of COVID-19 on Maldives food imports. However, due to COVID-19 there has been challenges for Maldives to export raw fish. This was a result of decline in demand of hotels in foreign countries and global slowdown of economic activities stemming from COVID-19.
indicator: Ability of international food supply chain to support domestic food availability

justification: Domestic food transport in Maldives is weak as it is made of 1200 small islands. Most islands are about 1 km small which makes logistic a challenge regardless of Covid.  Info gap as there are no reports of how locally sourced food supply chains operated. However, media reports claimed that food delivery by local stores to people's houses were encouraged by the government on 16th April. This ensured that people stay indoors and not spread COVID-19 related infections.

According to Human Rights Commission of Maldives the data for up to 30th April reveals that 88% people faced food shortages while the current food needs of 26% people were not fulfilled. Migrant workers were specifically affected with food shortages. Furthermore, staple food prices have also been hiked. The overall reason for food price hike is related to shortages of food products. However, an info gap has been marked as there is no clear indicator if the impact was driven  COVID-19.

In general, migrant workers in Maldives face deceptive recruitment practices, wage theft, passport confiscation, unsafe living and working conditions, and excessive work demands. These labour abuses indicate forced labor and violate domestic and international standards. Due to COVID-19 and the impact of lockdown the previous labour abuses has been exacerbated. As of July 3 statement by migrant workers, they are still facing abuses like  trafficking, forced labor, sub-minimum wages, involuntary and unpaid overtime, wage theft, and squalid living conditions. Human Rights Watch (HRW) even claims that 95 migrant workers who were living in one such congested and shared accomodation tested positive for the novel coronavirus. Furthermore, many such workers could not afford one full meal in a day, medical care or toiletries . This has resulted in protests by the workers. Workers have been stigmatised as politically motivated and a threat to national security. Discrimination also included non-payment of their salary since December 2019.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

Although the measures taken are less stringent than in other countries, domestic violence in Nicaragua has followed the same course observed in most other countries.

justification: In comparison to most other countries, Nicaragua has not adopted any confinement measures. The deteriorating mental health situation in the country is therefore due to the growing fear of contagion, also due to the way in which the authorities are managing the pandemic in the country, and mainly concerns those who have lost family members due to COVID-19 or those who are healed. According to a survey published in May 2020 by the Nicaraguan Foundation for Economic and Social Development (FUNIDES), 62.1% of the people surveyed recently have had some type of socio-emotional illness due to the pandemic. The survey shows that 19.6% of the Nicaraguans surveyed have had sleep disorders, blood pressure uncontrolled 8.3%, anxiety 7.4%, depression 6.7%, nervous breakdown 5.3%, panic attacks 3.2%, among other conditions. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) reported that mental health situation of migrants and IDPs has heavily deteriorated due to the health emergency.

The FSM government approved the economic stimulus package (US$15 million) and the Pandemic Assistance Program  (US$36 million) in April for a period of 9 months. These included wage subsidies, debt relief, and tax rebates.

justification: In July 2020, InSight Crimes reported that the Nicaraguan National Police has recorded the seizure of enormous amounts of money from drug trafficking while the seizure of cocaine is reduced compared to previous years; the provenance of this money is uncertain. This suggests that transnational drug trafficking have adapted to the COVID-19 emergency and they have not stopped their activity in the region, according to the source. Although drug trafficking does not appear to have significantly decreased due to the COVID-19 pandemic, as reported by Urban Violence Research Network (UVRN), local surveys have shown that drug dealers' activity has fallen sharply due to the economic impact of COVID-19, as well as the fear of contagion that drives people to stay home. Some drug dealers have reported making "home deliveries" ensuring interpersonal distance, but confirming that drug use in the country has significantly decreased due to the novel-coronavirus pandemic. The driver of this change is therefore behavioral, as economic activity is also a consequence of the closure of shops and commercial activities due to the fear of contagion, as no governmental restrictive measures have been implemented during the state of emergency.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: Nicaragua has one of the worst rates of prison overcrowding in Latin America, according to an analysis by World Prison Brief. The detention conditions are also among the worst in the region. Between April and May 2020, Nicaragua released more than 4,515 prisoners. In addition, 1,605 inmates were released in mid-July. The releases included elderly inmates and those with chronic illnesses, but official sources made no reference to COVID-19 as the cause of this decision. According to Amnesty International, the lack of drinking water, medical assistance and the drastic situation of overcrowding pose a great risk of infection n Nicaraguan prisons. Moreover, political prisoners face discrimination, being subjected to worse treatments and higher sentences than other prisoners, thus increasing their vulnerability to dengue fever and novel-coronavirus.

justification:
In May 2020, health workers and political activists expressed serious criticisms of the government’s pandemic response (the Nicaraguan Government did not impose a quarantine or preventive and restrictive measures in order to prevent and control the spread of the novel-coronavirus). The reason of the President Ortega's strategy was that confinement measures would have led the country's economy to collapse. 
Nevertheless, only two demonstration events directly related to COVID-19 were reported in the country until June: one of them, the state-sponsored “Love in Times of COVID-19” march in Managua on 14 March, intended to demonstrate solidarity with countries affected by the pandemic. According to ACLED, the march also served as a message, to the country and to the world, that the Nicaraguan government is opposing to social distancing rules. Dissent has been severely punished by the Nicaraguan Government, rendering public demonstrations particularly dangerous in the country.

justification: Media reports reveal that despite the school  opening from July 1st , the school  breakfast programme will be discontinued as a safety measure from COVID-19.

Communications from Maldives presidential office reveal that those who were in formal jobs would be provided with national health insurance, subsidised electricity and water.  As of 29 th March 104 complaints have been received by the Maldives job center to report employment terminations, no-pay leaves, pay cuts, allowance cuts, half-payments, and temporary employment suspensions. Moreover, the finance minister of Maldives has also promised a 3 month stimulus pay package for those who lost their jobs due to COVID-19. As of April 2nd 2020, 292 people have been terminated from employment due to the impacts of the novel coronavirus.

Women form 40 % of informal workforce in Maldives. Most of them are engaged in home-based-work. Since they completely depend on market forces for their daily wages they are facing poverty.  They are not able to make use of government social security benefits . Since resorts were temporarily stopped between April- June 2020 those who were working on informal contracts did not have employment for that period. Younger age group people who were on temporary contracts were most affected.

According to media reports various amendments to labour laws have been made. That includes, signing and providing an employment agreement between employer and employee, probation period limited to 3 months, redundancies based on specific conditions under the law, severance package for employee, 30 sick leave yearly, at least 10% service charge for those working in tourism, and introduction of minimum wages.  Additionally, limits were set on countries on the number of migrant workers coming to Maldives . However, there are no indications if these amendments are a result of COVID-19.

From March, schools in Japan were asked by the former Prime Minister Abe Shinzō to close until the next academic year. Generally speaking, majority of Japanese schools did not implement any form of remote learning during school closures. One of the most important reasons are cultural as Japanese culture prefers face-to-face communication which will enable them to look others in the eyes. As such, many of the school merely gave their students printed materials to work at home. According to a survey cited from NHK (Japan's only public media organization), merely 5% of local governing bodies planned some sort of online classes. In the meantime, some of the schools are closing down their gakudō (after-school clubs) programs (guaranteed in the 1997 Child Welfare Act). Note that Gakudō is a public funded service that requires a certain amount of monthly payment for schools to look after kids after school for working parents.

However, there are scarce instances where local councils have decided to proceed with local elections eg. Luzern despite the general agreement that Elections would be postponed due to COVID-19.
indicator: Elections taking place as scheduled pre-COVID

justification: According to the report by WFP survey in April, 48% of respondents reported loss of jobs or reduced salaries due to the lockdown and border closure. In May, Now Grenada news also reported that Government have been preparing guideline documents to provide safeguards for workers in private sector because a number of employers have already terminated workers contracts or reduced the salary of workers who continue to work

indicator: Migrant workers leaving to work abroad

justification: According to the OECD, long term or permanent residents/citizens of Switzerland are exempt to the entry ban implemented due to COVID-19. Therefore, migrant workers who have permanent residence in Switzerland have not been affected by the entry ban implementation due to COVID-19. However, there is a lack of data addressing the number or change in number of migrants who have returned from abroad to Switzerland.
indicator: Return of migrant workers  from abroad

justification: The Federal Statistic Office reported that Switzerland saw high excess mortality rates in the first few weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic (16 March-19 April). For example between 30 March-5 April, Switzerland saw 39% more number of deaths registered than average.
There is currently no information on the implications of COVID-19 on the population's access to reproductive services in Switzerland.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: Grenada's economy highly depends on the tourism, which have high proportion of informal workers. This sector was hit hard by the national lockdown and border closure. In addition, according to the report by WFP survey, people working on farming and fishing were also impacted because of the movement restriction. Since March 2020, the Government of Grenada had to implemented the COVID-19 Economic Stimulus Package, which provided payroll support payments, income support payments and support for small businesses
source: Caribbean Business Report, WFP, Now Grenada

justification: It was reported in May by some media sources that Grenada government was developing the documents to guide private sector treatment of workers amidst COVID-19. However, the finalised document could not be found anywhere at the moment, therefore, this indicator has been marked as an infogap
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

justification: News reports suggest that there has been a decrease of 30 million gallons (113,562,353 litres) of water per day, due to the heat and COVID-19, resulting in neighbourhoods of Santiago city and its surrounding towns. BNamericas points out that the newly elected government plans to invest in the water infrastructure system to address the fact that almost half of the population lacks access to clean water, and more than 76% of municipalities lack adequate infrastructure.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification: News reports describe hygiene products such as soap and toilet paper being sold out in anticipation of the arrival of COVID-19 in the country. Additionally, access to female sanitary products was also affected as a result of scarcity and an increase in prices.
indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: News reports indicate that prices of female sanitary products have increased as a result of the pandemic. Separately, prices of washing products and intimate hygiene products have reportedly increased by approximately 20% - 30% (source: Proceso).
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Whilst it is possible that there has been a change in the number of migrant returning from abroad, information could not be found confirming this, focusing only on the plight of migrant workers leaving the Dominican Republic. Therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.
indicator: Return of migrant workers  from abroad

justification: News reports point out that the Central Bank states the price of a basic basket has decreased. However, other articles suggest that prices of foods such as kidney beans, cassava and oil have increased, despite overproduction and excess supply stemming from the pandemic. Separately, currency exchange rates have also driven prices of imported pasta and oil up. In light of conflicting information, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

News reports indicate that the country's maternal mortality rate increased 27% in the first 6 months of 2020, compared to 2019 figures. However, the possible drivers are not identified, making it difficult to ascertain the impact of COVID-19 in this indicator. Therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.
Presidential elections were originally scheduled for May 2020. However, officials postponed the elections to July 2020 in light of the pandemic.
indicator: Elections taking place as scheduled pre-COVID

justification: No data could be found for the number of emigrants in 2020 as of 22 October 2020 - the latest data being from 2019. Therefore, this indicator has been marked with an InfoGap.

justification: The country's location as a narcotics transhipment point means that criminal organisations (both domestic and international)  are active in the country. However, the country does not have non-state armed groups controlling swathes of territory. Therefore, this indicator has been marked as Not Applicable.
source: Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance - International Security Sector Advisory Team

justification: Egypt suffered from a stockout of all medication. Indeed, the country is heavily dependent on imported medication and the pandemic slowed down economic transactions. In addition, the population and manufacturers started to stockpile over the fear of shortage and the latter preferred to sell their products to the black market at a higher price.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: According to UNFPA, many pregnant women refuse or delay medical appointments over the fear of catching the novel coronavirus. Moreover, Professor Dr. Mohamed Kamel, from the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Alexandria, expects that the pandemic would exacerbate shortage of medical equipment, and delay treatments and diagnosis for diseases other than the COVID-19.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: There is no information on how the avaliability of non-COVID-19 medical supplies has been impacted by the pandemic and measures implemented by the CAR government
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification:
No informations available regarding the COVID-19 impact on immunization campaigns in CAR. 
A media source reported that WHO announced that, in Central African Republic (CAR), two successful vaccination campaigns helped to curb the spread of measles in the country. A total of 2.6 million children were immunized in the vaccination campaigns, with particular emphasis on children aged between six and 59 months.
There is no information on the increase or decrease of mental health issues in CAR.
There is no information on the increase or decrease on alcohol consumption or substance use in the Central African Republic.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification: According to the FAO Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations, the food security of the population has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-July 2020). This is due to the strict measures on the closure of borders in CAR has prevented the inflow of goods such as food from entering the country. Food insecurity in CAR has been therefore aggravated by the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic; about 2.4 million people in the country are now facing food insecurity or acute food insecurity, which represents about an 11 percent increase compared with the pre-pandemic scenario, according to the IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification).
source: FAO Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations

justification: Humanitarian partners assisting in Afghanistan has increased in terms of active donor funding and NGO on the ground in response to the government's action plan. However their operations now have to account  for more people than ever.  For example 5 million more people have gone into food poverty due to unequal distribution of food by the government which means humanitarian organisations now have to access a larger group, this is challenged by the government imposed restriction son movement thus making it more difficult to reach remote regions as described by a Telegraph report.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification: The population's access to humanitarian assistance has decreased since the start of the pandemic. This change is driven by governmental change- the increased border restrictions and limited transportation has led to increased hardship accessing humanitarian services. This includes programs such as NGOs setting up 'Hygiene points' across different regions, or workshops/ safehouses for victims of domestic abuse. Due to travel restrictions and also fear of contracting the virus (Behavioural change), many families have been confined to their vicinities and households thus limiting their access to humanitarian services.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification: Public service funding in Afghanistan has significantly decreased since the start of the pandemic in March. This change is driven by government measures, initial public service budgets were concentrated around the country's health system and priming  the fragile system for the rising number of cases. However as the months progressed the health sector stayed the primary recipient of public funding. This was also focused on providing PPE across all sectors and increasing WASH sector services but neglected sectors such as education and agriculture.

The quality of public services provided by the government has significantly decreased since the beginning of the peak of the pandemic in March. This is driven by government measures such as unequal public service funding, insecurities and inadequate facilities. Furthermore this has caused  fear and feelings of danger for those accessing these facilities. Ongoing conflict and the recent hospital gun attack paired with improper PPE has made many people unsafe and thus decrease the quality of essential public services.

Foreign aid funding from INGO's and International donors has increased since the start of the pandemic to help protect Afghans and respond to the pandemic. The World Bank approved a $200 million grant in july to mitigate the impacts and provide relief to vulnerable people for example securing access to clean water and providing PPE.

National and local NGO programming in Afghanistan has decreased since the start of the pandemic. This change has been causes by funding shortages resulting from behavioural changes and government measures directing  funding to other avenues and cutting back of staff. Limited staffing and funding has drastically cut programs and staff on the ground working on existing programmes. However campaigns dealing with Covid-19 have emerged in place- for example increased number of campaigns spreading awareness about the symptoms of Coronavirus, how to mitigate the impact and prevention guidance.

This is flagged as Info Gap since no data of internal displacement can be found. Yet, number of internal migrants was recorded throughout the years updated monthly. The number of inter-prefectural (or provincial) migrants in April were 167,000 when the state of emergency was declared.
indicator: Internal Displacement and Mobility related to COVID-19

justification: According to the Foreign Minister, 250,000 Russians returned to Russia in March, April and May. The media reported that this was because Russians felt safer in Russia during the pandemic.
indicator: Return of migrant workers  from abroad

justification: There is a lack of data on the numbers of migrant workers leaving. Nearly all of the conversation centres around the lack of migrant workers in Russia due to the pandemic, leading to a labour shortage notably in Moscow (see link for example source).
indicator: Migrant workers leaving to work abroad

justification: In March, Putin declared a nationwide forced paid holiday leave for the month of April to stop the spread of COVD-19. However, in April, the media reported a lack of funds to support workers resulting in three common situations. The first was workers being dismissed sometimes illegally. The second was workers being forced to take unpaid leave or face dismissal and the third was employers reducing wages or hours worked. Furthermore, Putin signed the decree No. 274 which eases migrant workers' access to labour in Russia. Foreign workers do not need to re-register and they do not need permits for jobs from 15th March until 15th June to help combat the labour shortage resulting from the pandemic.
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

justification: Reports have shown that  the COVID-19 pandemic has caused the largest non-food product price increase to occur in hygiene/sanitisation related products in Switzerland. For example, Sanitisers have seen price increases of 2.4% between February-March 2020 followed by soap and toilet roll paper. There have also been reports of inflated consumer prices of face masks and hand gels in individual pharmacies.
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Inflation has increased by 2.87% since the beginning of the year. March and April saw the highest increase in inflation with it reaching 0.83% in April. The pandemic led to three changes in prices: an increase in the cost of medicine, a slight decrease in the cost of transport and a continuing unclear situation for services requiring physical contact.

Curfew, lockdowns and checkpoints imposed by Israel and Palestine prevent many Palestinians to access to non-related to COVID-19 health cares In the West Bank and East Jerusalem. 
In Gaza, from March to May, the Ministry of Health suspended all elective surgeries and medical procedures. In September, during the second lockdown, many public primary health care centres had to close. According to the NGO Refugees International, crossing closure to prevent the spread of the virus "have hampered access to life-saving healthcare for hundreds of Gazans resulting in loss of lives among non-COVID-19 patients".
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification:
Due to transport restrictions, in response to the fight against the novel coronavirus, Palestine lacks already scarce essential medical supplies. The UNRWA reported difficulties in importing lifesaving medication to noncommunicable patients. Indeed, national lockdowns in exporting countries, such as India, disturbed international trade.
The situation remains the same in Gaza, already under Israeli blockade, where there is an acute shortage of essential medicines "as the number of drugs categories at zero stock has reached 244 out of 516" according to Gaza Ministry of Health.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: Due to lockdown and movement restriction measures, vaccination campaigns were interrupted in Gaza. However, they resumed in September and Measles, Mumps, Rubella vaccine was provided.

There is lack of evidence to address whether COVID-19 has had implications on sewage or infrastructure treatment services in Switzerland. However, the Water Research Institute has reported on the detection of coronavirus in the sewage system.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification: The Swiss Federal Council has decided on financial measures amounting to 60bn CH in an effort to reduce the economic implications COVID-19 is having on the economy, unemployment, businesses and public services. For example, the federal council has compensated self-employed individuals who have suffered financial loss due to COVID-19 with an 80% compensation of total income being offered.
There have been small protests against the handling of the coronavirus pandemic outside of government buildings.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: On the 13th of March the Stockholm region expanded infection control care related to COVID-19 to include everyone. According to the decision, persons who are otherwise not covered (mainly vulnerable EU-migrants, Rumanians) by the right to free sampling, care and treatment for infectious diseases, will now also have the right to this in the same way as registered.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: This is Not Applicable, as there is no known child labour in Sweden.

There is a lack of data addressing the rate of primary school enrolment in 2020 in Switzerland as a result of implications caused by COVID-19. The latest evidence reporting primary school enrolment rates is based on 2018.

Consumer Food Prices in the month of March 2020 have decreased by -0.3% compared to the same month last year but showed an increase of 0.7% in food prices compared to the previous month  have. April 2020 saw a 0.7% increase in prices compared to March 2020. Increases in food prices have been consistently seen up to July 2020 where a decrease in food prices was observed.

The latest data on personal remittances could be found for 3.95% of GDP for 2019 (theglobaleconomy.com). There's no information on the change in this indicator could be found in 2020, therefore, it has been marked as an info gap

According to a factsheet about Grenada in Covid-19 by OCHA, the poverty rate in Grenada was relatively hight at 37.7%. However, it was not clear about the timing of this figure. No further reliable data on changing in poverty rate during Covid-19 in Grenada could be found. Therefore, this indicator has been logged as an infogap

Originated in 1993, The Technical Intern Training Program (TITP) is a governmental level labor program signed with developing countries to meet the shortage of labor force in Japan. Yet, it has been receiving criticisms over how it simply transformed the foreign trainees into cheap and disposable sources of labor. During the height of COVID-19, many foreign trainees were facing unemployment, lack of information regarding disease controls, etc while many of them worked in hard-hit manufacturing and food and hospitality industry sectors. However, On April 17 the government did make significant lossening in allowing the foreign trainees to seek another employer if unable to continue with the original employments under the "designated activities visa" up to one year's extension. It is flagged as Info Gap as there is no source of information to be found upon the the change of human trafficking or migrant smuggling specific to COVID-19.

Migrant smuggling and irregular migration has decreased during COVID-19, although is expected to change.

In regards to human trafficking and sexual exploitation, it decreased at the start of COVID-19. However, human trafficking and sexual exploitation has increased as of May 2020.
This is an info gap, as data is not available for 2020, only 2019.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

According to girlsnotbrides, there is no publicly available government data on child marriage in Grenada. No data on child marriage in since the pandemic began could be found either, therefore this indicator has been marked as an infogap

justification:
According to the FAO, measures put in place by the CAR government to try help curb the spread of the novel-coronavirus through border closures and movement restrictions have exacerbated the slowdown in food commodity imports and there has been a major disruption in the food supply chain in the country (March-May 2020). 
The majority of the imports are now coming from Cameron due to the closure of borders with other countries, however, the mobility restrictions between Cameroon and CAR are leading to substantial delays in food supply, which are responsible for shortages in the supply of oil, rice, soap and wheat.
indicator: Ability of international food supply chain to support domestic food availability
source: FAO Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations

justification: There is no information on how logistics in the domestic food supply chain have been affected in Central African Republic.

According to the FAO, people's access to markets in Central African Republic has decreased since the beginning fo the COVID-19 pandemic (March - August 2020), due to the disruption of basic services that was observed during the pandemic in the country, as well as the depletion of food stocks, rising staple food prices, the adoption of negative coping mechanisms by nearly half of the population and increased dependency on food aid.
source: FAO Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations

justification: No available information on how the labour force in domestic food supply chain has been affected in CAR.
indicator: Domestic food supply chain (available labour force)

justification: No data on how the COVID-19 pandemic measures have affected school feeding programmes in CAR.

According to the OCHA, the employment and livelihoods of those working in the formal sector have decreased since the beginning of the pandemic (March-August 2020), due to job loss or reduced income as well as because of the increased living costs related to the pandemic, thus affecting their livelihoods.

There is a lack of information on the impact of COVID-19 on informal employment in Central African Republic.
However, CAR has seen a rise in the creation of jobs through the mass production of face masks which has provided livelihood to about 18000 tailors who have been recruited to 300 local firms contracted through a local project, according to The World Bank.
No information on the amendments to labour laws in Central African Republic.
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections

The impact is logged as localized as the available documentation only refers to the Nicaraguan-Costa Rican boarder.

justification: The COVID-19 outbreak and its rapid spread caught many governments and agricultural producers by surprise causing a disruption  of the food supply chain.

justification:
According to media, in Jan 2020, US and UK officials have called on the Government of Grenada to undertake legal reform that will protect children against forced labour concerning the reports of domestic violence and child abuse in Grenada. However, there's no information on the changes in child labour in Grenada during covid-19 could be found, therefore, this indicator has been marked as an infogap
https://www.thestkittsnevisobserver.com/us-uk-call-on-grenada-to-end-forced-child-labour-gender-discrimination/

According to media, during the COVID-19 lockdown, the Grenada National Council of the Disabled (GNCD) have actively distributed over 270 food hampers to people with disabilities throughout the tri-island state. In addition, the St Andrew Development Organisation (SADO) collaborated with GNCD by finding elder people throughout vulnerable communities in need of assistance and then pass the list to GNCD so that they can deliver some 
 necessary items including raised toilet seats for the elderly. The GNCD is also working along with other government departments like the Ministry of Carriacou and Petite Martinique Affairs, to ensure that the elderly and disabled individuals are not left out.
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support

justification: No information about any COVID-19 related demonstration or rally could be found, therefore, this indicator has been marked as an infogap
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: According to a local media, the flow of personal remittances to Nicaragua has decreased since the beginning of the novel coronavirus pandemic (March-May 2020), due to the reduced income and higher levels of unemployment that followed the economic crisis due to the Governmental measures implemented at the international level to control the spread of the novel-coronavirus.

Although UNICEF indicates a possible increase in child labour in Nicaragua, as a secondary impact of the COVID-19 emergency, there are still no precise data or information regarding the trend of this indicator since the beginning of the pandemic.

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO) report published in September 2020, the household disposable income in Nicaragua has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-August 2020), as a consequence of the job loss in the formal and informal sectors, reduced flow of remittances, and lower job opportunities.
Also, according to a survey published by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in August 2020, the household disposable income of refugees in Nicaragua it was almost halved -from 93% of the surveyed households reported having a paid job before the pandemic (March 2020) to 59% (July 2020)- as a result of the work loss and the economic crisis following the restrictive Governmental measures implemented during the COVID-19 emergency.

According to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) report "Impact of Covid-19 on access to contraceptives in the LAC Region" published on August 2020, the access to family planning services is decreased since the beginning of the novel-coronavirus pandemic (March-July 2020). The cause of this change has not been indicated, and it is therefore logged as "undetermined". No accurate informations are available on maternal health services during the pandemic in the country.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification:
No reliable data are available on the poverty rate following the COVID-19 impact on the country's economy. The indicator is logged as info gap. 
Estimations regarding the change of this indicator are provided by The World Bank, the poverty rate in Nicaragua will increase to 15.1 percent in 2020 (from 9.7 percent in 2017), adding more than 350,000 people into poverty.

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO) report published in September 2020, the formal employment is decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-August 2020), as a consequence of the current economic crisis. The drivers of this change are unclear as it has not been specified if it depends on behavioral changes (self-lockdown) or governmental measures implemented during the COVID-19 emergency.

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO) report published in September 2020, the informal employment is decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-August 2020), as a consequence of the current economic crisis. As reported by ILO, the factors influencing the trend of this indicator are the absence of social security (access to health insurance and / or professional risks), being of low income, and concentrated in the sectors most affected by the crisis.

According the Instituto Nacional de Información de Desarrollo (INIDE), the monthly inflation (June 2020) increased (Consumer Price Index (CPI) registered a monthly inflation of 0.75 %) compared to the same period from last year (0.09% in June 2019). The driver of the change was not indicated and has therefore been logged as "undetermined".
source: Instituto Nacional de Información de Desarrollo (INIDE)

justification: In Nicaragua, school remained open (March-August 2020) despite the health emergency. Thus, according to the Economic Commission of Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), distance learning programmes have not been implemented. Government of Nicaragua, instead, provided guidelines on health habits.
source: Economic Commission of Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC)

justification: No data are available regarding the trend of the primary school enrollment in 2020 in the country.

According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), many Nicaraguans migrants in Costa Rica have been forced to return to their country of origin, due to unemployment and income loss (March-August 2020). source: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)

justification:
According to a media source, population's access to humanitarian services or assistance to the Indigenous Population (medical assistance, sanitation measures, lack of transparency of COVID-19 related informations) has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-June 2020), due to the lack of Government support.
Furthermore, as reported by Amnesty International, inmates in Nicaraguan prisons lack of clean water and medical assistance (March-August 2020).

indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification: According to a media source, the provision of clean water to the population has decreased in Nicaragua since the beginning of the pandemic (March - August 2020), due to increased demand for provision of WASH-related services during the health crisis, and due to the already existing fragility of the WASH infrastructure in the country, especially in rural areas. The driver of the change of this indicator is therefore behavioral.
indicator: Provision of infrastructure related to water, sanitation and hygiene

justification: According to a local media, the prices of personal hygiene and sanitation products in Nicaragua have increased (between 10% and 15% in April 2020), since the beginning of the novel-coronavirus pandemic (March-April 2020), due to an increase in demand of these products. More precise or recent informations are not yet available.
indicator: Prices of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: Although some IO/INGO reported the redirection of their humanitarian aid, to be delivered in Nicaragua during the COVID-19 emergency, according to The New Humanitarian, the Nicaraguan government has limited the presence of international aid. The trend of the indicator is therefore "undetermined".

According to the World Food Programme (WFP), staple food prices (beans and maize) experienced a severe increase since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-July 2020). The reason of this change is, according to the source, panic-buying that was observed at the beginning of the state of emergency.

According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) report "Impact of COVID-19 on Nicaraguan PoC" published in August 2020, food insecurity with regard to PoC persons of concern has decreased since the beginning of the pandemic (March-July 2020); the driver of the change is undetermined. No informations available at the national level (localized impact).
source: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)

The West Bank is more impacted than the Gaza Strip. Indeed, contrary to the laster, the former's economy depends on private sector (tourism, construction...), and not on the public sector, which was less disrupted.

During the lockdown period, the informal sector, which employs 48% of Palestinian, was the most affected and a large proportion of workers lost their income and their job. The transport, construction, restoration, tourism and retail-trade sectors were the most impacted.

According to UNDP April report the Maldives Correctional Service identified 105 prisoners who have almost completed sentences for minor crimes, who were pardoned by President Solih on 18 April 2020 under the Clemency Act, to protect the health of prisoners and officers. In addition, Maldives Police Service announced changes to the procedure to visit inmates in Maldivian prisons following the declaration of a state of public health emergency over the ongoing COVID-19.

According to May 2020 government report, COVID-19 has directly impacted over 91,000 school children (from pre-KG to higher secondary). Learning  has been interrupted, more so for the more vulnerable children of Maldives. Students who were pursuing lower levels of the education system have had the longest interruption of learning. It was recorded that the postponement of examinations at the end of grade 10 will affect the transition of some of these youngsters to higher secondary and tertiary level studies for some of them. Depending on the institutions chosen, this may mean losing a full year of studies at a critically young age, affecting, among other factors, the interest for higher studies.  Based on a survey carried out by the Ministry of Education (Maldives) in March 2020, it was found that over 31% of the audience (students, teachers and parents) did not have access to the internet or Wi-Fi at home. Some students also did not have the relevant devices. This meant a programme via the medium would not benefit a significant number of children.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools
