indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification:
According to a media, the access to non COVID-19 related health services has decreased since the beginning of the novel-coronavirus pandemic in Brasil (March-April 2020). 
According to the source, non-urgent operations and treatments (COVID-19 unrelated) have been postponed during the health crisis.
Moreover, the media reported that behavioral changes also impacted the access to health services, due to the fear of contracting the novel-coronavirus, while attending hospitals and health centers. This factor mostly concerned pregnant women and patients with cardiac problems.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification:
There are only scattered reports on interruptions of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies; as of October 2020, no major disruptions have reported.
The New York Times reported the reduced access to medical supplies for malaria, HIV, and tuberculosis in Brasil, amid COVID-19 pandemic (March-August 2020), due to restrictions in international transport. The availability of these medical supplies is particularly challenging for populations living in remote places, like in the Amazonian state.
indicator: Availabilty of non-COVID-19 related medical supplies

justification:
A local media reported that the novel-coronavirus has caused collapses in health systems in Brasil during the COVID-19 emergency (March-May 2020). According to the source, vaccinations have been postponed or suspended in some parts of the country. Moreover, indications to stay home and the fear of the population to contract the novel-coronavirus while attending health centers are preventing people from vaccinating.
Alarmed by the decline in vaccination coverage, authorities created in April 2019 Movimento Vacina Brasil, with the aim of increasing immunization coverage and fighting misinformation around the country; people over 60 years old and health workers were prioritized in this immunization campaign.

The Government of Brasil reported an increase in mental health issues (anxiety, post-traumatic stress, and, to a lesser extent, depression), related to the impacts of the pandemic in terms of uncertainties and lifestyle changes (due to social distance and other containment measures) (March-September 2020).  
As of August 2020, FAPESP (Sao Paulo Research Foundation) reported as increased depression among health workers (67%), compared to the same period in 2019 (20%), and an increased level of anxiety (52% of health workers affected) compared to 40% in 2019.

According to a Research Institution, in Brazil alcohol and tobacco consumption increased (April-May 2020) compared to the period before the COVID-19 pandemic. Between April and May, there was a general increase in alcohol consumption of 17.6% (18.1% for men and 17,1% for women). According to the source, this increase was highly co-related with feelings of sadness and depression due to COVID-19 pandemic impacts.
The same report also reveals a rise in tobacco consumption between April and May 2020; the figures of increased use of tobacco are higher for women.
indicator: Alcohol consumption and/or other substance use

justification:
According to local media sources, UN agencies reported that food insecurity is increasing due to the the COVID-19 pandemic, mostly because of the increasing unemployment and the increase in basic food products (rice, beans) in August and September 2020, in Brazil.
As of September 2020, Inter Press Service reported that the food insecurity situation -which already grew from 2013 to 2018 (by 62.4%)- has aggravated due to agricultural policies, and the reduction and misallocation of government emergency aid.

In March 2020, media sources (Jornal do Comercio, The One Brief) called attention to the challenges "short chains" faced to get to consumers (mainly small scale farmers). 
Another media source (Brasil Debate), as of May 2020, reported disruptions in the logistic structure in the country, due to the restrictions on movements implemented by the authorities. The huge distances of the country and the dependence on roadways (60% of food is transported by road) make food chains especially vulnerable to changes (mobility restrictions, truck drivers being at risk population, facilities along the way closed, etc.).

According to a local media, many local food markets closed in Brazil (April-May 2020), due to the novel-coronavirus pandemic, directly affecting smaller-scale producers and their distribution networks.

A report by PwC released in April 2020, remarks disruptions in supply chains in Brazil, also due to quarantines of truck drivers. It also highlights the impacts of social distancing in labour-intensive activities of the sector, which highly depends on (national and international) labour that has seen more difficulties to move and settle in these locations.
Another article in Brasil Debate published in May 2020, calls attention to the lack of labour force due to the pandemic in the CEASAS (supply centrals), mainly due to the high dependence of Food Banks on the military and on volunteers to distribute the food. It reported that the lack of workforce in food supply chains, could mean throwing away food in good conditions while there are growing numbers of people in need.
indicator: Domestic food supply chain (available labour force)

justification:
According to the World Food Program (WFP) in Brazil over 40 million children are missing school meals due to school closures. Nevertheless, in April 2020 the Government of Brazil implemented the PNAE (Programa Nacional de Alimentação Escolar; national school feeding programme) through an adaptation to the COVID-19 context (April-October 2020). Instead of meals in school, food kits were given to parents or tutors by the local council in charge.
Media sources called attention on how this new modality is impacting the quality of the food distributed to families. The PNAE normally takes an important share of its products from family farming, but now that the entities have to stock and distribute the food kits, fresh products from this type of agriculture are harder to add to the meal, affecting the quality of the meals and the quantity of nutrients provided to children.
source: Fundo Nacional de Desenvolvimento da Educação (FNDE; national fund for education development)

justification:
According to the (IBGE) Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, employment and livelihoods in the formal sector have been severely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, mostly due to national and international mobility restrictions (April-June 2020). According to the IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics) unemployment rate was at 13.3% in the second trimester of 2020  (Apr, May, Jun), compared to the fourth trimester of 2019.
According to the same source, in June four out of the 10 companies that stopped their activity reported doing so due to the pandemic, and 70% of firms reported a general negative impact.
There are also important differences between states, with higher rates of unemployment in the Northeast of Brazil.
source: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica (IBGE; Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)

justification:
According to the According to the (IBGE) Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, employment and livelihoods both in the informal sector have been severely affected by the pandemic, mostly due to national and international mobility restrictions and social distancing measures. Of the 8.9 million of jobs loss in this period, 6 million belonged to the informal sector, as reported by the IBGE.
According to the same source, the informality rate reached 37.4% of occupied population for the period May-July 2020 (30.7 million informal workers). In the same trimester in 2019, the informality rate was 41.3%. 
There are also important differences between states, with higher rates of unemployment in the Northeast of the country.
source: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica (IBGE; Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)

justification:
Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-April 2020), a series of temporary measures were taken to protect employment in Brazil. Another important measure to help informal workers and the unemployed is the reinforcement of Family Fund (Bolsa Familia Programme), and the creation of an emergency aid programme (Auxílio Emergencial), which provided monthly cash transfers to the most vulnerable.
Note that source date is not available.
indicator: Amendments to labour laws or worker protections
source: Brazilian Government (Ministério da Cidadania - citizenship's ministry)

justification:
There is no data yet for personal remittances as a percentage of the GDP for 2020, making difficult proportioned comparations. Last figure was for 2019, according to the World Bank personal remittances accounted for 0.175% of the GDP, a figure that peaked an increasing trend since 2017.

Despite in the first months of the pandemic the World Bank projected a decrease in remittances as a result of COVID-19 outbreak, other data show the opposite trend. The Brazilian Central Bank estimated an increase of remittances to Brazil, following a greater recovery of other countries in relation to Brazil from the socio-economic impact of the COVID-19 (Correio Braziliense).

According to the (IBGE) Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, monthly inflation rate for September 2020 was of 0.64%, the highest for 2020. This increase was mainly due to the rise of food prices (meat, rice, soy oil, milk) and gasoline. The sector of services (healthcare, education) is still in deflationary trends, visibly affected by the pandemic.
source: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica (IBGE; Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)

justification: Fundação Getúlio Vargas reported that in Brazil, poverty rate (below US$5.50/day) as of June 2020 was at 21.7% and extreme poverty (below US$1.90/day) at 3.3%. These figures represent an important decrease compared to the same period of last year (25.6% and 8.0% respectively), The change of this indicator is caused by the economic stagnation that followed the restrictive measures implemented by the Government in order to control the spread of the novel-coronavirus in the country.

According to the Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica (IBGE), as of September 2020, 24,2% of the working population in Brasil, received a lower income compared to the period prior to the novel-coronavirus pandemic (March-September 2020). Another factor that is affecting negatively the household disposable income in Brasil, is the important rise in unemployment observed during the COVID-19 state of emergency.
These figures do not consider government subsidies, which have become crucial during the COVID-19 pandemic, especially for poorest people.
source: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica (IBGE)

justification:
According to UNESCO, access to primary and secondary education facilities in Brazil decreased since the beginning of the pandemic (March-September 2020), due to school closures, affecting 16.106.812 primary school students and 23.118.179 secondary school students, a total of 39.224.991 students.
According to a local media, by August and September 2020, some states have implemented a gradual return to schools, mainly focusing on pre-primary schools and tertiary education. Despite these efforts, there has been a lot of heterogeneity and lack of agreement between states (e.g., Amazonia had to close again due to an increase of novel-coronavirus cases).
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

justification: Although there has not been an unified remote learning response from the Brazilian authorities during school closures due to the COVID-19 pandemic (March-August 2020), schools have started to implement distance learning programmes, reaching 91% of Brazilian children, as reported by UNICEF. Nevertheless, important inequalities are made visible and widened, as many students do not have the resources to follow distance learning programmes (e.g., no access to internet, connectivity). Moreover, there are many differences between private (19% of families) and public schools in the implementation of the online learning modality.

There are no reports on the impacts of COVID-19 pandemic on child marriage in Brazil.

According to UNICEF in 2017 11% of girls by 15 years-old were married, and up to 36% of girls by 18 years old, making that of Brazil the fourth highest number of child brides in the world (3,034,000).

In legal terms, the minimum age for marriage is 18, but both girls and boys who are 18 years old can marry with the consent from either parents or their legal representatives in Brasil. Moreover, until 2019 (when the new law passed), minors under the age of 16 could marry in case of pregnancy or to avoid a criminal sentence for statutory rape.

In May 2020, the FBSP (Brazilian Forum of Public Security) reported that feminicides increased by 22.2% since the beginning of the lockdown measures (March-May 2020), compared to the same period in 2019; also, domestic violence cases reported on the emergency line increased by 27%. There has been a decrease of reports in physical aggressions  (-25.5%) and decreased reports of rape (-28.2%) compared to 2019, which according to the source, reflect a difficulty in reporting aggressions events to police stations during the COVID-19 emergency.
The drivers of this increase in domestic violence during the pandemic are related to people being isolated with their agressors and the limitations to access protection and report networks.
source: Forúm Brasilero da Segurança Pública (Brazilian forum of public security)

justification:
According to a media source, since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-June 2020), it has been reported an increase of discrimination and targeted violence against the Asian population, due to the effects that the pandemic had on xenophobia.
Furthermore, as reported by the BBC in Mato Grosso and by the Guardian in Pará, there was an increase in discrimination against Indigenous communities during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Finally, the Forúm Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (Brazilian forum of public security), reported a rising discrimination against the Afro-descentent population in the country, and especially those belonging to the poorest quintiles of the population and/or living in favelas.
indicator: Discrimination or targeted violence against marginalised groups

justification:
No clear informations about migrant smuggling or human trafficking have been retrieved for Brazil in 2020. 

A UN report, published in May 2020, alerted about the potential increase of human trafficking and migrant smuggling due to the COVID-19 pandemic-related mobility restrictions implemented by the authorities.
Due to the economic and health impact of the pandemic in Brazil, many people originally from Venezuela and Haiti are attempting to migrate to Chile (through Brazil), during the health crisis. There are only scattered informations about the movement of migrants from Brazil to Chile during the COVID-19 emergency.

A local media reported that from March to May 2020 child labour has increased in Brazil (653 inspections have verified child labour cases), compared to the same period in 2019 (in which only 176 child labour cases were confirmed).
In a research conducted by Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT, public work in ministry) in a partnership with UNICEF revealed an intensification in child labour, which increased of 26% from May to July 2020 in Sao Paulo.

According to an Academic Research Institute, Brazil's great social inequalities, and racial discrimination (against migrants, poor or Black communities), have translated in an unequal access to COVID-19 related support (March-May 2020). 
The source also reported that Infrastructure and geographic specificities are also crucial, regarding for instance access to health services in favelas or the existence of the long distances and barriers to access hospitals in remote places.
Observatório de Favelas also reported unequal access to health services in Rio de Janeiro (informations based on statistics and health workers narratives).
indicator: Access for minorities or specific groups to COVID-19 related support
source: Instituto de Saúde Colectiva (colective health institute)

justification:
According to a media, since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-October 2020), there have been an increasing number of demonstrations across the country, mostly protesting issues related to the COVID-19 management from the national authorities. 
Even if there were particular confrontations between protesters and with authorities, demonstrations in general were not violent.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest related to COVID-19 response

justification: A media reported that, since the beginning of COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrations pro and against the Brazilian President Bolsonaro occurred across the country. Social unrest events have been linked to anti-fascist and anti-racist movements. These latter have been especially emphasised with the murder of George Floyd in May, the subsequent Black Lives Matter movement, and the racial inequalities in Brazil, that have been exacerbated during the COVID-19 pandemic (March-June 2020.
indicator: Demonstrations/civil unrest unrelated to COVID-19 response

justification:
According to government data published in October 2020, in Brasil, the rate of imprisonment fell in the first half of the year, compared to 2019. Media reports call attention to the difficulties of preventing COVID-19 disease, as well as the lack of informations regarding the spread of the novel-coronavirus, in Brazilian prisons.
It is remarkable that there are important variations in incarceration rates and overcrowding rates between different states.

Since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-May 2020), media, organisations, and academic researchers (UFPel, ORCID) report an increase in events of physical and mental violence to health workers, mainly due to an increased fear of the population of contagion from the novel-coronavirus.
Moreover, other reports refer to institutional violence due to the high numbers of health professionals infected and dead due to the novel-coronavirus in the country. By the end of May, according to COFEN (Conselho Federal de Enfermagem, federal council of nursery), Brazilian infected health professionals accounted for up to 40% of world-scale cases of COVID-19 among health workers. Aggressions by the population, and the lack of sanitary protection adds to the long working hours, and psychological impacts of the pandemic.
source: Journal of Nursing and Health, Nursing Faculty (Federal University of Pelotas)

justification:
As reported by Human Rights Watch and InSight Crime, an increase in human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies was reported since the beginning of the COVID-9 pandemic in Brazil (March-June 2020). Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo's favelas saw police violence surge with the pandemic despite crimes dropped dramatically (precisely due to isolation measures). Human Rights Watch reported that in the first four months of 2020, police in Rio de Janeiro killed 606 people, a 43% increase from the same period in 2019. In June 2020, Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF, Brazil's supreme court) ordered that police halt their operations in the overcrowded and poor favelas. Nevertheless, media ( O Globo) reported that violence events during police operations in favelas continued to occur. O Globo reported in June that police in the state of Sao Paulo killed 381 people between January and April 2020, showing an increase of 30% in police killings compared to 2019.
These increase and alarming rate of killings in police operations are linkable to COVID-19 pandemic, as it justifies a greater presence of enforcing agencies.
indicator: Human rights abuse and violations by enforcement agencies or other authorities

justification:
Events of hostile language and discriminations from authorities have increased in Brazil since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic (March-June 2020), as reported by a media. 
Events of discrimination against Chinese population by an Brazilian authority occurred at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Discrimination against indigenous communities also increased during the health crisis, as reported by the BBC in Mato Grosso and by the Guardian in Pará, there has been an attempt from local authorities to implement confinement measures only for Indigenous communities in June 2020.
indicator: Hostile language or stigmatisation against a specific group by authorities

justification:
According to media sources, privatizations of public services were already a priority of the minister Guedes (who came to power in 2019), but this has been emphasized by the economic crisis that followed the restrictive measures implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic (March-September 2020). 
In June 2020, measures to ease privatization were approved by national authorities, particularly with regard to the WASH sector. State-owned Eletrobras (producer and distributor of electric energy) is at the center of discussion over privatization; Correios (postal service) has been privatized in September 2020.

UN agencies have redirected their efforts toward the COVID-19 emergency in Brazil, as well as many INGOs like Manos Unidas, REMAR, International Amnesty, etc. (March -June 2020)
Despite from this information, it was reported by a media, that in August 2020, national authorities have prevented Medecins Sans Frontiers (MSF) to act in an Indigenous community who had been seriously affected by COVID-19.
The overall change of this indicator is logged as increased.

No clear informations available regarding the programming of local/national NGOs amid the pandemic in Brazil. 

There are scattered reports that show certain activities have had to be canceled due to sanitary measures (for instance, Todos pela Educaçao). Moreover, it can be expected that mobility restrictions, indications to stay home, and the crisis would have negatively impacted NGOs, and especially smaller ones. Those still active, on the other hand, are expected to shift their efforts towards the COVID-19 response.

UN agencies, did not report major difficulties in accessing people in need during the COVID-19 pandemic in the country. 
As reported by a media source, in August 2020, Medecins Sans Frontiers (MSF) was stopped by Brazilian authorities from providing humanitarian support and assistance to Indigenous communities heavily affected by the COVID-19 pandemic in Mato Grosso. This change is therefore due to Governmental Measures.
indicator: Humanitarian access to people in need

justification:
No informations available regarding the population's access to humanitarian services or assistance during the COVID-19 pandemic in Brasil. 
Lack of access to communication in remote areas has been highlighted by organizations like Saúde e Alegria and Medicins Sans Frontiers (MSF). Also, police interventions in favelas have interrupted humanitarian services, as reported by InSight Crime and Human Rights Watch.
indicator: Population's access to humanitarian services or assistance

justification:
Non-state armed groups in Brazil are mainly related to drug trafficking and paramilitary groups. 
A research study of Universidade Federal Fluminense revealed in October 2020 that about 20% of the metropolitan region in Rio de Janeiro was controlled by non-state armed groups. This authority has also been visible during COVID-19. In March and April 2020, there are reports of Rio drug trafficking and paramilitary groups imposing a curfew in the favelas. Despite this information, the trend of this indicator (compared to the period prior to the pandemic) is undetermined.

Media sources (Agencia Brasil, Universo On Line) reported shortages of alcohol gel and protective masks, due to the increased demand of these products ( end of February 2020 - March 2020).
UNICEF, in partnerships with other actors, has been distributing kits with basic sanitary and hygiene products in favelas and metropolitan regions (March-July 2020). Other groups like Saúde e Alegria have taken similar initiatives in the Amazon region (Pará) with Indigenous and ribeirinhos communities.
indicator: Availability of personal hygiene and sanitation items

justification: According to National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), the access to other preventive, curative and emergency health services (elective procedures, non essential surgeries) has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-September 2020); they have been canceled or delayed as efforts have been redirected to COVID-19 case management, and due to the limited number of medical personnel and hospital beds for intensive care. As reported by the source, this change is also due to the hesitancy of patients to seek care due to fear of the novel-coronavirus.
indicator: Access to other preventive, curative, and emergency health services

justification: According to UNICEF report released on August 2020, family planning and maternal health services (maternal and child health, prevention and treatment of gender-based violence (GBV), sexually transmitted infections) have decreased during the COVID-19 emergency (March-June 2020), due to the existing weaknesses in the national health system, further worsened during the COVID-19 case management.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services

justification: According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), livelihoods of the part of the population participating in informal work in Ecuador has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 emergency (March-June 2020), due to increased unemployment rates (that followed the restrictive governmental measures implemented during the pandemic). In particular, migrants and refugees, who are over-represented in the informal sector, are among the most affected.
source: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) through Reliefweb

justification: As reported by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), discriminations and xenophobia events against migrants and refugees, have increased since the beginning of the novel-coronavirus pandemic in Ecuador (March-June 2020). Since March, all Palestinian universities had to close due to lockdowns and went online. The situation is of concern in the Gaza Strip were many students (up to 40% in some universities) dropped out as a result of their inability to attend online lectures. In the West Bank, schools closed mid-March to prevent the spread of the novel coronavirus and provided online learning and TV broadcasts. For the new school year that started in September, schools under the Palestinian Authority Ministry of Education, the UN Relief and the UNRWA reopened in two stages. First, students from grades one to four and the 12th grade attended in-person lessons followed two weeks later by the rest of the pupils. Each student will only attend in person three days a week and two days remotely. Some schools had to close again in October amid new cases. 
In the Gaza Strip, schools closed on the 5 March , and lessons were broadcasted on the radio and online. Schools reopened in September for the new school year but had to close again following a new COVID-19 outbreak. 
In East Jerusalem, schools are under Israeli supervision. They closed on March, but while on 3 May the Israeli authorities reopened schools, Palestinian schools decided to remain closed (except for 12th-grade exam) and provide e-learning. As classrooms are overcrowded and they have no mean to ensure physical distancing. They reopened in September but quickly closed again amid an Israeli national lockdown. 

However, across Palestine, many do not possess a computer or a tablet and do not have access to the internet, which prevent children from accessing online academic content.
indicator: Access to primary and secondary schools

There is no exact data for the number of migrant workers leaving Brazil in 2020. Nevertheless, media reports suggest in the last years there has been an increasing tendency of Brazilians to leave to work abroad; other media also suggests this trend was emphasized during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In 2019, different media (G1, El País) reported a trend of Brazilians leaving to work abroad, especially to Portugal, Canada and Japan. These media suggest the political situation in the country has considerably affected these decisions.

Different media sources also reported an increasing will among Brazilians to travel abroad to live/work during the COVID-19 pandemic. Nevertheless, the closure of frontiers has prevented many to move abroad. According to a media source, leaving Brazil illegally has been an option during the health crisis.
indicator: Migrant workers leaving to work abroad

justification:

Last available data for mortality rate was of 6.5 deaths per 1000 inhabitants in 2019, according to Knoema.

This figure is expected to increase considerably with COVID-19 pandemic, as of October 2020, Brazil has the fourth highest mortality rate in the world due to COVID-19 disease: 75.02 deaths per 100.000 as reported by RTVE, based on data by the World Bank and Johns Hopskins University.

According to Sistema de Alertas Regional (regional alerts system), the access to sexual and reproductive services has decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil (March-July 2020). Many non-essential health services were suspended during the pandemic (among which family planning and maternal health services). Moreover, the population and especially pregnant women showed reticence in accessing health centers due to fear of contagion from the novel-coronavirus. 
Furthermore, the Brazilian government, as reported by Human Rights Watch, has dismissed legal abortion services during the pandemic.
indicator: People's access to sexual and reproductive services
source: Sistema de Alertas Regional (regional alerts system)

justification:

This trend also includes schools, of which about 39% do not have access to basic sanitary infrastructures, directly affecting COVID-19 prevention. Nevertheless, there are wide disparities across the country (states in the Amazonian region are especially affected).

COVID-19 pandemic is expected to decrease school enrollment rates at all education levels.

Media reports inform that many Brazilian migrants and travellers found themselves stuck in the first months of the pandemic and were unable to return to Brazil (March-May 2020). Since the start of the pandemic, the Brazilian government has organised a series of repatriation flights, prioritising Brazilians that were abroad temporarily.
Reasons of the return to Brasil during the pandemic are related to the precarious working and living conditions that these migrants face with COVID-19 sanitary and economic crises. 
Poder360 (newspaper), based on data from the IOM, reported that in Portugal the great majority (93%) of migrants requesting to return to their country are Brazilians, and that these requests have increased by 32% in the first semester of 2020 compared to that of 2019.
The trend of this indicator is logged as undetermined.

Lake Chad Basin and Tibesti.

The rate of poverty in 2020 has increased due to restrictions put in place to stem the spread of COVID-19 which have had economic consequences, notably during the national lockdown. The national poverty rate, measured as the actual subsistence rate in Ukraine, is projected to be 45% at the end of 2020. In 2019, the forecast for 2020 was a poverty rate of 31.2%.

For the new academic year, small groups of 15 to 20 pupils have been formed to ensure that physical distance is respected, and they will only be able to go to school three times a week. Half of the 30 hours of classes will be face-to-face, and the other half will be distance learning. In addition, the choice was given to the parents, either to send their children at school or to opt for e-learning. The Minister of National Education, Vocational Training, Higher Education and Scientific Research announced that 80% of them chose to send back their children at school mainly due to the bad experience many had during the first school closure from March to July. justification:
The number of food insecure people in Brasil in 2020 is not available yet.

UN agencies expect COVID-19 pandemic to negatively influence food security in the region of Latin America and the Caribbean. Moreover, unemployment and the rise of food prices in Brazil have been particularly remarkable, potentially affecting food security of the population.

The IBGE (Brazilian institute of geography and statistics) published in September 2020 the data for 2017-18. These data revealed hunger grew in the country in the last 5 years and food security aggravated for the first time in 2018.
